0025a62a-84a8-49ba-a85e-4223ff05c364.paragraph: The Beyneu Compressor Station on the Beineu–Bozoi–Shymkent gas pipeline is the most likely source of this 559 t/hr TROPOMI methane plume detected on 8 October 2024. The station sits 16 km SSE (upwind) of the detection point — wind that day was from the SSE at 6.4 m/s, placing the plume directly downwind of the compressor station with only a 5° bearing deviation. The same location has been detected emitting methane persistently by at least four satellite instruments (EMIT, Carbon Mapper/ISS, GHGSat, and TROPOMI) across more than 30 separate overpasses between August 2022 and April 2026, at rates typically ranging from 300 to over 20,000 kg/hr, confirming a chronic, multi-year emission source. The compressor station, commissioned in 2015 as the starting point of the Beineu–Bozoi–Shymkent trunkline, lies within a dense cluster of gas pipeline substations and industrial infrastructure south of Beyneu town, with no alternative large sources (landfills, coal mines) present in the search area.
0025a62a-84a8-49ba-a85e-4223ff05c364.source_label: Beyneu gas compressor station, Beineu–Bozoi–Shymkent pipeline

1206309-3324.paragraph: An unnamed industrial works facility mapped as oil and gas infrastructure within a large industrial landuse area is the likely source of the 847 kg/hr methane plume detected by GHGSat-C2 on 19 February 2022. The plume sits just 200 m from a mapped 'man_made=works' node and within an industrial compound containing a chimney and numerous storage tanks. Wind at the detection hour was from the north at 0.8 m/s, consistent with the source lying slightly upwind (56 m north) of the detection coordinate. The area has a dense detection record — 199 satellite observations from multiple sensors between 2019 and 2025 — with a tight cluster of repeat detections centred on the same facility complex, confirming a persistent emission source. The surrounding wells in the Wetherbee, Keg Shell, and Potato Baby lease areas are operated by COG Operating LLC, making it the most probable operator of the unnamed facility.
1206309-3324.source_label: Unnamed oil and gas works, Delaware Basin, Texas

12585.paragraph: The methane plume detected by GHGSat-C1 on 30 September 2022 is most consistent with the sabotaged Nord Stream 2 pipeline (Pipe A) in the Danish exclusive economic zone south of Bornholm. The detection coordinate (54.8762°N, 15.4100°E) matches the documented DANGER AREA 1 exclusion zone (54.8767°N, 15.4100°E) established by Danish maritime authorities after the 26 September 2022 explosions — an offset of only ~55 metres, well within GHGSat's accuracy. Three GHGSat satellites (C1, C2, C4) imaged plumes at this site on the same day, consistent with the intense post-sabotage monitoring campaign. The measured emission rate of ~84 tonnes per hour aligns with a high-pressure transmission pipeline rupture; the four Nord Stream leaks together released an estimated 150,000 tonnes of methane. Wind from the SSW at 6.2 m/s is consistent with the plume geometry, with the southernmost detection upwind of the two northern detections.
12585.source_label: Sabotaged Nord Stream 2 pipeline in Baltic Sea

14373.paragraph: The methane plume detected by GHGSat-C6 on 29 May 2023 is most consistent with emissions from the Szyb III Poniatowski ventilation shaft of the KWK ROW underground coal mine in Jankowice, Poland. The plume origin (50.0309, 18.5722) sits just 150 m from the shaft, with wind from the NE carrying the plume toward the detection point; 15 separate satellite detections from GHGSat, Carbon Mapper, EMIT, and EnMAP cluster tightly around this shaft between 2023 and 2025, with eight explicitly classified as coal-mine sources. Global Energy Monitor researchers independently attributed plumes at these exact coordinates to the KWK ROW mine's ventilation system, and a February 2026 Ember analysis documented repeated methane venting from drainage systems at the Jankowice unit at rates of 1,000–1,800 kg/hr — consistent with the 1,774 kg/hr observed here.
14373.source_label: Ventilation shaft Szyb III Poniatowski, KWK ROW mine
14373.source_name: Szyb III Poniatowski KWK ROW Ruch Jankowice

1792403-20715.paragraph: The KU H production platform (KHPB) and associated well cluster in PEMEX's Ku-Maloob-Zaap offshore oil field is the likely source. The GHGSat detection at 62 t/hr on 2023-11-20 is positioned 0.24 km northwest of the KU H platform complex, aligned near-perfectly with the wind from the southeast (134°) at 7.7 m/s at the detection hour — consistent with plume drift from the platform to the detection point. This location has been detected 164 times by multiple satellites (GHGSat, IMEO/Landsat, IMEO/Sentinel-2, IMEO/EMIT) between 2022 and 2026, with four GHGSat overpasses in a single week in November 2023 recording rates from 13,000 to 62,000 kg/hr, indicating a persistent, massive methane source from routine offshore production operations such as gas venting or incomplete flaring. The Ku-Maloob-Zaap complex is Mexico's largest oil field, operated by PEMEX, producing substantial volumes of associated natural gas.
1792403-20715.source_label: KU H production platform, Ku-Maloob-Zaap offshore oil field
1792403-20715.source_name: KU H Producción KHPB, Ku-Maloob-Zaap Field

24575.paragraph: A municipal solid waste landfill or dump site is the most consistent source for the 2,707 kg/hr methane plume detected by GHGSat-C8 on 15 January 2024 in southern Vadodara, Gujarat. The location has been detected 43 times by GHGSat between February 2022 and February 2024, with emission rates ranging from 114 to 2,707 kg/hr — a level of persistence and variability characteristic of landfill methane. The GHGSat detections cluster in two spots roughly 400 metres apart, with a clear temporal shift from the northern cluster (all detections in early 2022) to the southern cluster (dominant from late 2022 through early 2024), a pattern consistent with waste placement moving between cells of a landfill operation. The site sits on the southern outskirts of Vadodara near the Vadodara Bypass (NH 48), where municipal waste infrastructure is typically sited, and no oil and gas facilities, coal mines, or mapped industrial sources are present in the vicinity. The specific facility name could not be confirmed — the location is unmapped in both the OGIM inventory and OpenStreetMap — but the emission pattern and local context are most consistent with a municipal solid waste disposal site operated by or serving the Vadodara Municipal Corporation.
24575.source_label: Municipal solid waste landfill, southern Vadodara

25efba54-83e0-40fe-b972-b9860d1d0a80.paragraph: The ~37 t/hr methane plume detected by TROPOMI on 2 March 2023 is most consistent with emissions from the KWK Jas-Mos underground coal mine, located 4.2 km east of the detection in the Upper Silesian Coal Basin. Although the mine was officially closed on 31 December 2022 and transferred to SRK for restructuring, ventilation systems typically remain operational during early-stage liquidation, and abandoned deep mines in gassy coal seams can continue to emit methane at high rates. A second TROPOMI detection of similar magnitude (33 t/hr) was recorded 1.9 km from the mine, and wind from the northeast is broadly consistent with the plume being detected west-southwest of the facility. The rate — equivalent to 37 tonnes per hour — is characteristic of mine ventilation shaft emissions and far exceeds what any landfill or industrial facility in the area could produce.
25efba54-83e0-40fe-b972-b9860d1d0a80.source_label: KWK Jas-Mos coal mine ventilation (under liquidation)

27421a7d-113c-41a0-9363-b10869eb13a8.paragraph: The methane plume detected by TROPOMI on 8 November 2025 is most consistent with aggregated emissions from the Hassi Messaoud oil field, Algeria's largest oil field operated by Sonatrach, producing approximately 350,000 barrels per day. The detection sits over a dense cluster of more than 80 petroleum wells mapped in OpenStreetMap within a few kilometres, with surface winds from the south-west that day pointing to sources upwind of the TROPOMI pixel centre. Satellite archives contain 199 methane detections within 30 km since 2023, including a tightly clustered series of high-resolution observations (Carbon Mapper Tanager, Sentinel-2, PRISMA, EMIT, EnMAP, Landsat) concentrated at a point 1.5 km NNW that confirm a persistent chronic source — likely an industrial oil facility (OSM way/695838035) and adjacent well pads — though at rates of 0.1–4 t/hr, far below the TROPOMI estimate of roughly 650 t/hr. The TROPOMI rate, with its large 7 × 5.5 km pixel, likely integrates methane from multiple well pads, pipelines, and processing infrastructure across this mature supergiant field, though the coarse resolution precludes attribution to a single facility.
27421a7d-113c-41a0-9363-b10869eb13a8.source_label: Hassi Messaoud oil field infrastructure, Sonatrach

344d38d9-7256-4dcc-96a8-6fde8f3f3956.paragraph: The Gadap Town landfill complex on the outskirts of Karachi is the most consistent explanation for this methane plume. Detected by TROPOMI on 8 November 2025, the plume's rate of approximately 984 tonnes per hour (±505 t/hr) is characteristic of a megacity landfill — Karachi generates over 16,000 tonnes of municipal waste daily, most of which is disposed at the Jam Chakro and Gond Pass landfill sites in Gadap Town. The UN IMEO/MARS analyst classified the detection as 'waste' sector, and the WNW wind places the source upwind of the detection coordinate, consistent with the Gadap Town landfill area. With 199 TROPOMI detections recorded across the area between 2023 and 2025 — at rates consistently between 46,000 and 181,000 kg/hr — the site ranks among the most persistently observed methane hotspots in the global satellite record, strongly indicative of a large, active landfill with sustained anaerobic decomposition. The TROPOMI sensor's ~7 km footprint precludes pinpointing a single cell within the complex.
344d38d9-7256-4dcc-96a8-6fde8f3f3956.source_name: Gadap Town landfill complex (Jam Chakro / Gond Pass)

3f4e3b75-7949-4dcb-b72c-3f505f1d341d.paragraph: The Shondoni Coal Mine, an underground operation in Sasol's Secunda complex, is the most likely source of this 19,000 kg/hr TROPOMI methane plume detected on 22 May 2024. The mine sits approximately 20 km northeast of the plume coordinate, and with surface winds from the NNE that day, its emissions would drift roughly toward the detection location — the 28° crosswind offset is within TROPOMI's km-scale uncertainty at this distance. Higher-resolution instruments confirm a persistent methane source at this mine: an EMIT detection (1,269 kg/hr) and multiple EnMAP detections (600–865 kg/hr) cluster 4–5 km south of Shondoni, consistent with a ventilation shaft, while a Carbon Mapper Tanager detection on 23 June 2025 placed a 1,372 kg/hr plume just 2 km from the mine coordinates. The mine produces 5.6 million tonnes of coal annually from underground operations at 155 m depth, and ventilation air methane from such a large underground mine can readily account for the observed emission rate. The broader area has 77 satellite methane detections between 2023 and 2025, underscoring the Highveld coalfield as one of the world's most persistent methane hotspot regions.
3f4e3b75-7949-4dcb-b72c-3f505f1d341d.source_label: Shondoni underground coal mine, Sasol Secunda complex

GAO20220627t163654p0000-A.paragraph: The 952 kg/hr methane plume detected by the Global Airborne Observatory on 27 June 2022 is most consistent with an oil and gas facility at 47.9699°N, 103.2070°W — the upwind (southwest) end of the imaged plume mask at the reported coordinates. A southwest wind of 3 m/s carried the plume northeast across the detection scene. Carbon Mapper classified the source as Oil & Gas (1B2), and the location sits in the heart of North Dakota's Bakken shale play where Oasis Petroleum North America LLC and other operators maintain dense well pads. However, neither the OGIM v2.7 inventory nor OpenStreetMap records any facility within 630 metres of the inferred source point — the nearest mapped wells are the Oasis-operated BERQUIST pad roughly 760 metres south. Given the aircraft sensor's 5–15 metre geolocation accuracy, the emitting infrastructure is almost certainly at the plume origin point itself and is simply absent from available asset databases. No repeat detections have been recorded at this exact location, suggesting an intermittent or one-off emission event such as a blowdown, maintenance activity, or temporary upset.
GAO20220627t163654p0000-A.source_label: Unmapped oil and gas infrastructure in the Bakken

GAO20240430t174249p0000-D.paragraph: The 297 kg/hr methane plume detected by the Global Airborne Observatory on 30 April 2024 is most consistent with emissions from an oil and gas tank battery at the Nailed It Federal Com well pad in Eddy County, New Mexico, operated by Civitas Permian Operating, LLC. The aircraft detection coordinate sits directly atop four storage tanks mapped in OpenStreetMap — just 10 metres away — and the plume's south-to-north orientation matches the southerly wind recorded at the time, confirming the tanks as the upwind source. This location has been detected emitting methane repeatedly: 17 Carbon Mapper aircraft and satellite overpasses between August 2023 and October 2024 measured rates ranging from 70 to 576 kg/hr, indicating a persistent, unmitigated source. The broader lease includes multiple active gas wells operated by Civitas Permian and a compressor station operated by Salt Creek Midstream 210 metres to the southwest, but the plume coordinate pinpoints the tank battery as the primary emission point.
GAO20240430t174249p0000-D.source_label: Oil tank battery at Nailed It Federal Com
GAO20240430t174249p0000-D.source_name: Nailed It Federal Com well pad / tank battery

a74ee5ec-094d-433f-bd5e-ca644aca86ac.paragraph: A gas flare at the Pazanan oil and gas field is the likely source of the 1,827 kg/hr methane plume detected on 15 September 2024. The detection coordinate sits just 20 metres north-northwest of a mapped flare stack (OSM node 5820568665) connected to a gas pipeline network, and light southerly winds (0.9 m/s) would carry emissions northward directly over the detection point. Seven additional satellite detections at the same location between June 2023 and November 2025 — recorded by EnMAP, EMIT, Sentinel-2, Landsat-8, and Carbon Mapper's Tanager — confirm a persistent, high-rate methane source, with rates ranging from 808 to 6,101 kg/hr. The Pazanan field, operated by the National Iranian South Oil Company, is a supergiant retrograde gas condensate reservoir producing 750 million cubic feet of gas per day, placing a flare stack of this scale well within the observed emission range. The repeated nature of the detections suggests chronic underperformance of the flare — either frequent periods of being unlit, low combustion efficiency, or routine venting of uncombusted gas.
a74ee5ec-094d-433f-bd5e-ca644aca86ac.source_label: Gas flare at Pazanan oil and gas field
a74ee5ec-094d-433f-bd5e-ca644aca86ac.source_name: Pazanan oil and gas field flare stack

a8f5f746-8b65-4f40-bdae-8b86edebf668.paragraph: No methane source capable of producing an 851,000 kg/hr plume could be identified within the 5 km search radius of this GOES detection in Canyon County, Idaho. The detection coordinate (43.74, −116.60) lies in a rural residential area along Ember Road north of Middleton, with wind from the northwest placing any potential source in an area of scattered homes, farms, and open fields. No oil and gas infrastructure, landfills, coal mines, or industrial facilities appear in the OGIM, OSM, or coal mine databases within 5 km, and the nearest mapped features — a small Republic Services waste-disposal node and Intermountain Gas Company distribution markers — sit 4.2–4.5 km downwind in the opposite direction from where wind would place a source. The extremely high emission rate, absence of repeat detections, and lack of any plausible local source raise the possibility of a detection artifact from the GOES sensor, which is not purpose-built for methane quantification.
a8f5f746-8b65-4f40-bdae-8b86edebf668.source_label: no identifiable source within search radius

ang20170616t210522-H.paragraph: A dairy manure management system (likely an anaerobic lagoon) is the most likely source of this methane plume, detected by Carbon Mapper's AVIRIS-NG aircraft on 16 June 2017. The plume was measured at 264 ± 55 kg/hr at 36.1594, −119.2829 in Tulare County — the leading dairy county in the United States. The detection provider classified the source as Livestock (IPCC 4B), and the nearest mapped infrastructure is a 248-acre confined animal agriculture operation (OSM way 131195886) located 0.6 km NNE, well-aligned with the NNE-to-SSW wind recorded at the time. The site has been repeatedly detected by AVIRIS-NG and the Global Airborne Observatory across 2016–2024, with rates ranging from 35 to 452 kg/hr — a persistent pattern consistent with ongoing manure management emissions. No active oil and gas infrastructure or coal mines exist within the search radius.
ang20170616t210522-H.source_label: Dairy manure management operation near Avenue 204, Tulare County

ang20180922t205612-Q.paragraph: The 696 kg/hr methane plume detected by AVIRIS-NG on 2018-09-22 is most consistent with emissions from the Sentinel Peak Resources Welport well pad in the Cymric Oil Field near McKittrick, Kern County. The reported source coordinate sits just 28 metres downwind (SW) of the Welport 81 and Welport 80 cyclic steam wells, with wind from the northeast at 5 m/s at the time of detection — placing the source directly at this well pad. This location has registered 199 methane detections across eight years (2017–2025) from multiple airborne sensors, with rates ranging from 38 to over 1,800 kg/hr, confirming a persistent, high-emitting oil and gas source. A 2019 California Air Resources Board audit identified 287 methane leaks on Sentinel Peak Resources equipment statewide, and the company's steam generators in the Cymric field have received 14 violation notices for leaking since 2017, according to San Joaquin Valley air district records.
ang20180922t205612-Q.source_label: Sentinel Peak Resources Welport 81 cyclic steam well pad
ang20180922t205612-Q.source_name: Welport 81 (Welport well pad, Cymric Oil Field)

ang20200825t203650-A.paragraph: An active oil and gas well pad in California's Elk Hills field is the likely source of this 92 kg/hr methane plume. The AVIRIS-NG airborne sensor pinpointed the plume, and the detection-hour wind from the NNE places the source at the NNE end of the imaged plume mask — within 40 metres of wells 52W-35R and 42N-35R, both operated by California Resources Elk Hills, LLC. This location has been detected 13 times by aircraft between 2017 and 2020, with emission rates ranging from 47 to 522 kg/hr, confirming a persistent methane source at this well pad. All detections in the cluster are classified as oil and gas sector emissions.
ang20200825t203650-A.source_label: Elk Hills oil field well pad, wells 52W-35R and 42N-35R

cfe180de-3067-4caf-a033-4a5a9bfc7ff2.operator: KazTransGas (subsidiary of KazMunayGas), Gazprom-controlled CAC system
cfe180de-3067-4caf-a033-4a5a9bfc7ff2.paragraph: The Beyneu (Oporanya) compressor station is the most likely source of this 265-tonne-per-hour methane plume. The station sits 3.4 km southwest of the TROPOMI detection centroid — well within the sensor's 5.5×7 km pixel footprint — at the strategic junction of the eastern and western branches of the Central Asia–Center gas pipeline system, one of the world's largest gas transmission corridors. A subsequent TROPOMI detection in October 2025 placed a 23-tonne-per-hour plume directly at the compressor station (within 140 metres), confirming the facility as a persistent and highly variable methane emitter. The daily-mean wind was from the south-southeast, and while a 3.4 km offset with an 86-degree bearing discrepancy from the ideal upwind direction suggests some uncertainty in plume transport or centroid placement, no other mapped infrastructure of comparable scale exists within the search radius that could plausibly generate an emission of this magnitude.
cfe180de-3067-4caf-a033-4a5a9bfc7ff2.source_label: Beyneu compressor station, CAC gas pipeline system
cfe180de-3067-4caf-a033-4a5a9bfc7ff2.source_name: Компрессорная станция Опорная (Oporanya / Beyneu Compressor Station)

emi20230814t100819p07019-A.paragraph: An offshore oil and gas platform in the Kazakh sector of the Caspian Sea, approximately 45.334°N 52.373°E, is the likely source of this 44 t/hr methane plume detected by Carbon Mapper on 14 August 2023. The location lies about 2–3 km west of the Buzachi Peninsula in the Mangystau Region, with SSE winds at the time of detection consistent with the plume extending NNW across the sea surface. This site is a persistent super-emitter: 21 satellite detections from four instruments (EMIT, PRISMA, EnMAP, and TROPOMI) were recorded between June and October 2023, with emission rates reaching as high as 210 t/hr. The precise-sensor detections (EMIT, PRISMA, EnMAP) all converge within 210 metres of the same offshore point, while TROPOMI detections scatter across the surrounding area as expected for its coarser resolution. The facility is not captured in the OGIM v2.7 inventory or OpenStreetMap, consistent with the poor coverage of offshore Caspian infrastructure in these databases; the specific platform or field name could not be confirmed through available searches.
emi20230814t100819p07019-A.source_label: offshore oil and gas platform, Kazakh Caspian Sea

emi20240217t052731p04010-A.paragraph: A ventilation shaft of the Sihe Coal Mine, one of China's largest and gassiest underground coal mines, is the source of this persistent methane plume. The detection cluster at 35.6084°N, 112.5282°E sits approximately 1.4 km NNE of the mine's main industrial complex and has been observed emitting methane across 19 high-confidence satellite detections from four sensors (Carbon Mapper, GHGSat, EMIT, PRISMA) between 2021 and 2026, with rates ranging from 4,000 to over 37,000 kg/hr. The Sihe mine, operated by Jinneng Holding in the Qinshui Basin, has a documented absolute gas emission rate of 486.6 m³/min and is classified as an outburst-prone mine; its CMM power plant captures high-concentration methane but roughly 40% of mine gas is low-concentration and vented. The TROPOMI instrument has also detected enormous plumes of up to 242,000 kg/hr within 1.5 km of this location, consistent with combined emissions from multiple ventilation shafts across the Sihe complex.
emi20240217t052731p04010-A.source_label: Sihe Coal Mine ventilation shaft, Qinshui Basin, Shanxi
emi20240217t052731p04010-A.source_name: Sihe Coal Mine (Jinneng Holding Equipment Manufacturing Group)

emi20240409t074435p05007-A.paragraph: A methane leak from the Southern Corridor (Южный Коридор) gas pipeline is the likely source of this plume. The plume, detected by Carbon Mapper/EMIT on 9 April 2024 at 48.8 t/hr, was located just 160 metres west of the pipeline — consistent with easterly winds (from 83°) pushing the plume downwind of the source. The Southern Corridor is a major Gazprom trunkline carrying high-pressure natural gas across southern Russia; a leak or maintenance venting from this pipeline, or from an associated valve station, would be capable of producing the very large emission rate observed. No other oil and gas infrastructure, coal mines, or landfills are mapped within the 3 km search radius, and the pipeline is the only plausible source matching the rate and sector classification.
emi20240409t074435p05007-A.source_label: Southern Corridor gas pipeline near Alekseyevskoye, Krasnodar Krai
emi20240409t074435p05007-A.source_name: Southern Corridor Gas Pipeline (Южный Коридор), section KS Shakhtinskaya – KS Korenovskaya

emi20240608t122634p08012-A.paragraph: Venting from oil and gas infrastructure in the Goturdepe field is the likely source of this 55-tonne-per-hour methane plume. The Carbon Mapper detection sits within a cluster of 29 other satellite detections—from IMEO, GHGSat, TROPOMI, and additional Carbon Mapper overpasses—all converging within 200 metres of the same coordinates on the Cheleken Peninsula between 2021 and 2025, at rates ranging from 3,000 to 40,000 kg/hr. WNW winds at the time of detection place the source upwind, consistent with the Goturdepe field operated by Turkmenistan's state oil company Türkmennebit. Independent research and a 2023 Guardian investigation identified this western Caspian coast as one of the world's largest methane hotspots, with the majority of super-emitter events traced to extinguished flare stacks venting unburned gas.

f2fd0ea9-3f92-486d-9062-5bf880c737db.paragraph: A natural gas pipeline is the likely source of this 162 t/hr methane plume, detected by EMIT on 14 February 2024. The plume sits directly above an underground gas transmission pipeline (OSM Way 538321219), with the wind from the SSW aligning the detection precisely downwind of the pipeline segment. On the same day, explosions described by Iranian officials as 'sabotage and terrorist action' struck this very pipeline — a 790-mile trunkline running from Asaluyeh to the Caspian Sea — with Iran's gas network control centre confirming blasts at several locations along the route. A second satellite sensor (Carbon Mapper) detected a 42 t/hr plume at the same coordinates, corroborating a major release event.
f2fd0ea9-3f92-486d-9062-5bf880c737db.source_label: Natural gas pipeline venting during Feb 14 sabotage

sron_20230916_37.09N_111.97E|SRON_Weekly.paragraph: Coal mining operations in the Jiexiu area of Shanxi province are the likely source of this 61,000 kg/hr methane plume detected by TROPOMI on 16 September 2023. The detection sits in one of China's most intensely coal-mined regions: 103 other satellite methane detections exist within 30 km, nearly all classified as coal-related. A cluster of five EMIT detections 2.7 km away at the Yi'an industrial rail hub, all tagged as coal by IMEO, confirms a persistent coal-methane source at that location. The very light SSE wind (0.3 m/s) means the plume remained close to its source, and TROPOMI's coarse 5.5×7 km footprint likely integrates emissions from multiple coal-related sources — mine ventilation, coal processing, and storage — associated with the Shanxi Jiexiu Xinyugou mining operations of Shanxi Luxin Energy Group.
sron_20230916_37.09N_111.97E|SRON_Weekly.source_label: Coal mine methane, Jiexiu Xinyugou complex, Yi'an

sron_20231020_37.67N_61.38E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The 483-tonne-per-hour methane plume detected by TROPOMI on 20 October 2023 over the Mary Region of Turkmenistan is most consistent with a major emission from gas infrastructure along the Central Asia–Center (CAC) pipeline corridor. The detection lies directly on the 1,422 mm CAC trunk pipeline, which transports gas from the Dauletabad and Shatlyk fields north toward Russia, and the NNW wind direction places the source upwind along this same pipeline. With 91 TROPOMI detections recorded within 30 km between 2023 and 2026—among the most persistent and intense methane hotspots ever observed from space—the area hosts chronic large-scale venting likely from compressor stations, processing facilities, or unlit flares operated by the state gas company Türkmengaz. No specific named facility could be identified from available mapping data, as Turkmenistan's gas infrastructure is sparsely documented in public inventories.
sron_20231020_37.67N_61.38E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Central Asia–Center gas pipeline system, Mary Region, Turkmenistan

sron_20240917_51.72N_56.24E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The КС Саракташ (KS Saraktash) gas compressor station, operated by Gazprom Transgaz Ekaterinburg on the Dombarovka–Orenburg trunk pipeline, is the likely source of this 440-tonne-per-hour methane plume. The station sits 4.8 km east (bearing 80°) of the TROPOMI detection, closely aligned with the ENE wind direction that would carry emissions toward the observed plume location. A prior GHGSat-C4 detection on 6 December 2022 measured a 1,833 kg/hr plume just 0.7 km from the compressor station, confirming it as a known methane emitter. The emission rate — equivalent to roughly 3.9 million tonnes per year if sustained — is consistent with a major operational blowdown or emergency venting event at a large gas trunkline compressor station, where pressurised gas is rapidly released to atmosphere during emergency shutdowns or maintenance.

sron_20241008_45.47N_55.09E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: A gas compressor station at the western terminus of the Beyneu–Bozoy–Shymkent trunk gas pipeline in western Kazakhstan is the likely source of this massive methane plume. The plume was detected by TROPOMI on 8 October 2024 at an estimated rate of 559 tonnes per hour, with surface winds blowing from the SSE — aligning the detection almost directly downwind of the compressor station, 16 km to the SSE. Satellite archives reveal that this facility has been one of the most persistently detected methane sources in Central Asia: over 40 detections by EMIT, Carbon Mapper, GHGSat, and TROPOMI between 2022 and 2026 pinpoint the same compressor station, with typical rates of 1–20 tonnes per hour. The exceptionally high TROPOMI rate on this date suggests a major operational blowdown or emergency venting event at the station, which is operated by KazTransGas and forms part of the Kazakhstan–China gas export corridor.
sron_20241008_45.47N_55.09E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Beyneu compressor station on Beyneu–Bozoy–Shymkent gas pipeline

sron_20241014_35.52N_112.69E|SRON_Weekly.paragraph: The Sihe No.2 Coal Mine in Zezhou County, Shanxi, is the likely source of this 57,000 kg/hr TROPOMI methane plume detected on 14 October 2024. A dense cluster of 27 high-resolution satellite detections (EMIT, Tanager, PRISMA, EnMAP, and Carbon Mapper ISS) spanning 2023–2026 pinpoints the emission origin at 35.543–35.546°N, 112.630–112.631°E — a location that Global Energy Monitor's methane emitters tracker explicitly attributes to this mine. On the same day as the TROPOMI detection, Carbon Mapper's ISS instrument measured 2,263 kg/hr and EMIT measured 8,339 kg/hr at this precise location. The mine is classified as 'gassy' (高瓦斯), operates underground with a 3 Mt/yr capacity across a 45.5 km² concession, and its persistent multi-year detection pattern across seven satellite instruments is characteristic of coal mine ventilation emissions.

sron_20250911_62.92N_75.21E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Oil and gas operations in the Pogramichnoye field are the likely source of this 542 t/hr methane plume, detected by TROPOMI on 11 September 2025. The plume sits squarely within the Surgutneftegas-operated field, where over 80 industrial well pads are mapped, and the IMEO processing pipeline independently flagged the same plume as oil-and-gas-related. A northerly wind (4.3 m/s) placed the source upwind of the detection coordinate, consistent with emissions from the dense cluster of well pads to the north. However, TROPOMI's 5.5×7 km pixel size prevents attribution to a specific well pad or facility, and the single-day detection — with no repeat in the satellite record — suggests a transient event such as venting, flaring, or a brief blowout rather than a persistent leak.
sron_20250911_62.92N_75.21E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Oil and gas operations, Pogramichnoye field
sron_20250911_62.92N_75.21E|SRON_Weekly_.source_name: Pogramichnoye oil and gas condensate field

sron_20251125_35.42N_51.32E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The Aradkouh landfill complex south of Tehran is the likely source of the 27,000 kg/hr methane plume detected by TROPOMI on 25 November 2025. The landfill, which receives roughly 10,000 tonnes of Tehran's waste daily, sits approximately 5 km north-northeast of the plume coordinate — consistent with the light northwesterly wind (0.1 m/s from 319°) that day. The attribution is strongly supported by an extraordinary detection history: 142 satellite observations within 30 km, including dozens of high-precision Carbon Mapper and EMIT detections (2023–2026) pinpointing the landfill at ~35.456°N, 51.332°E with rates of 1,600–8,500 kg/hr, all tagged as 'waste' by analysts. Academic studies identify Aradkouh as a major methane emitter and note that it lacks a gas capture system, allowing methane from decomposing organic waste to vent freely.

sron_20260527_41.43N_88.33W|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Aux Sable Liquid Products' natural gas processing facility in Morris, Illinois, is the most likely source of the 58,000 kg/hr methane plume detected by TROPOMI on 27 May 2026. Located 2.8 km southeast of the detection coordinate — well within the 5.5×7 km TROPOMI pixel — the facility is the largest natural gas processing plant in the United States, capable of processing 2.1 billion cubic feet of gas per day. The plant has a documented history of fugitive emissions: a 2018 EPA settlement found it had exceeded its VOC emission limits by approximately 27.5 tons per year since 2000 due to equipment leaks and faulty emission calculations, and it was required to implement enhanced leak detection and repair. The very light wind (0.6 m/s from the NNE) means the plume would have drifted only about 2 km, and Aux Sable is the only facility within range with the throughput to plausibly generate a 58 t/hr emission, likely from a process upset, emergency blowdown, or flare malfunction. No other satellite detections exist at this location in the 4-source archive, consistent with an intermittent operational event.
sron_20260527_41.43N_88.33W|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Aux Sable gas processing plant, Morris Illinois

sron_20260530_21.82S_148.47E|SRON_Weekly.operator: Coppabella and Moorvale Joint Venture (CMJV, majority Peabody Energy)
sron_20260530_21.82S_148.47E|SRON_Weekly.paragraph: The 23,000 kg/hr TROPOMI methane plume detected on 30 May 2026 is most consistent with fugitive emissions from the Coppabella Coal Mine, a large open-cut metallurgical coal mine in Queensland's Bowen Basin. The mine sits 5.2 km WSW — directly upwind of the plume coordinate under the day's WSW wind — and the plume is observed ENE of the mine, precisely matching the wind direction. Coppabella has a dense detection record: the 86-detection archive for this area includes 15 GHGSat point-source detections (600–3,200 kg/hr) clustered within 0.3–1.9 km of the mine's OSM boundary, Carbon Mapper and IMEO detections explicitly classified as 'coal', and four prior TROPOMI detections at 17,000–21,000 kg/hr. The mine reports 791,000 tonnes CO₂-equivalent in annual methane emissions under Australia's National Greenhouse and Energy Reporting scheme, and the Global Energy Monitor wiki associates multiple Carbon Mapper methane plumes directly with this facility.
sron_20260530_21.82S_148.47E|SRON_Weekly.source_label: Coppabella Coal Mine, Bowen Basin surface mine

sron_20260607_23.68S_46.60W|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: A specific source for this TROPOMI detection could not be confidently identified. The plume was detected over Diadema, São Paulo on 2026-06-07 at an estimated rate of 11,000 kg/hr, with surface wind from the WNW at just 0.8 m/s. Two landfills — Aterro Sanitário de Santo André (11.6 km east) and Aterro Sertãozinho in Mauá (12.9 km ESE) — are confirmed methane sources via repeat high-resolution detections from Carbon Mapper, EMIT, and PRISMA instruments, and all IMEO-classified detections in the region are labelled as the waste sector. However, both landfills lie downwind of the TROPOMI plume coordinate on this date, making them unlikely to be the source under the prevailing wind. The upwind corridor (WNW, toward Taboão da Serra) is predominantly residential and lacks any mapped landfill, wastewater treatment plant, or gas infrastructure capable of the observed emission rate. The 79-detection history (2023–2026) confirms a persistent large methane source in the São Paulo ABC region, but available evidence does not tie this particular plume to a specific facility.
sron_20260607_23.68S_46.60W|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Unidentified methane source in Diadema industrial district

sron_20260607_37.35N_61.93E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Gas processing infrastructure at the Galkynysh gas field is the likely source of this 23,000 kg/hr methane plume. The detection lies within Turkmenistan's Galkynysh field — the world's second-largest gas field — where 144 TROPOMI detections over a 30 km radius have recorded rates from 26,000 to 198,000 kg/hr, all classified by IMEO as oil and gas sector emissions. Light NE winds (0.8 m/s) on the detection date place the source a few kilometres northeast of the reported coordinate, consistent with one of the field's three major gas treatment plants (built by Petrofac, CNPC, and Hyundai/LGI) or associated well pads operated by state-owned Türkmengaz. No alternative sources (coal mines, landfills, or other industrial facilities) appear in the OpenStreetMap or OGIM inventories for this area. Turkmenistan has been independently documented as the source of 15 of the world's 25 largest methane mega-leaks, with its ageing gas infrastructure singled out as the dominant driver.
sron_20260607_37.35N_61.93E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Gas processing infrastructure at the Galkynysh gas field
sron_20260607_37.35N_61.93E|SRON_Weekly_.source_name: Galkynysh Gas Field gas treatment plants

sron_20260607_41.18N_69.08E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Gas distribution or storage infrastructure in the Yangiyul District of Tashkent Region is the most plausible source of this 18,000 kg/hr methane plume, though the specific facility cannot be identified from available data. The TROPOMI detection on 7 June 2026 sits within a well-known persistent methane hotspot: 164 satellite detections over three years form a tight cluster within 2 km of this location, with IMEO classifying the majority as oil and gas sector emissions. OpenStreetMap records multiple gasometers (including an underground gas storage tank 5 km upwind) and pipeline segments in the area, consistent with Tashkent's gas supply network, while no coal mines or large landfills are mapped near the plume origin. The very high emission rates recorded across multiple dates — ranging from 7,000 to over 100,000 kg/hr — are characteristic of gas infrastructure venting or leaks rather than agricultural or small industrial sources.
sron_20260607_41.18N_69.08E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Gas infrastructure in Yangiyul District, Uzbekistan

sron_20260607_54.88N_86.57E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The 23,000 kg/hr methane plume detected by TROPOMI on 7 June 2026 in Krapivinsky Municipal Okrug is most consistent with coal mine ventilation or abandoned mine methane from the Kuznetsk Basin (Kuzbass), one of the world's largest coal-producing regions. The detection sits in an area with 14 prior TROPOMI detections over 2023–2026, several of which the UN IMEO programme classified under its 'coal' sector, with rates ranging from 17,000 to 94,000 kg/hr — a scale characteristic of underground coal mine ventilation. NW winds place the likely source 2–10 km upwind of the reported coordinate, near a cluster of prior coal-tagged detections around 54.89°N, 86.47°E, though no named mine in the Global Coal Mine Tracker database lies within 30 km of that location, suggesting the emissions may originate from abandoned mine vents or shafts not catalogued in current databases. The British Geological Survey has noted that annual methane emissions from Kuzbass coal mines reach 1–2 billion cubic metres, with much coming from abandoned workings.
sron_20260607_54.88N_86.57E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Coal mine methane in the Kuznetsk Basin

sron_20260608_31.14N_49.36E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The 72,000 kg/hr methane plume detected by TROPOMI on 8 June 2026 is most consistent with emissions from the Marun 3 oil and gas processing facility, a large industrial complex operated by the National Iranian South Oil Company in Iran's Marun field — the country's second-largest onshore oil field. The facility sits 4.4 km west of the reported plume coordinate, within TROPOMI's expected 2–10 km source-offset range for its 5.5×7 km pixels. The attribution is strongly supported by a dense detection history: at least 29 methane plumes have been recorded at this exact facility cluster between August 2022 and November 2025 by EMIT, Carbon Mapper, EnMAP, and TROPOMI sensors, with TROPOMI-measured rates reaching 41,000–102,000 kg/hr — consistent with the scale of the current plume. The daily-mean wind on the detection date was from the northwest, which would ideally place the source north of the detection rather than west; this geometric offset tempers confidence somewhat, but the facility's multi-year, multi-sensor emission record makes it overwhelmingly the most plausible origin.
sron_20260608_31.14N_49.36E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Marun 3 oil and gas processing facility, Khuzestan
sron_20260608_31.14N_49.36E|SRON_Weekly_.source_name: Marun 3 Oil & Gas Exploitation Company (شرکت بهره برداری نفت و گاز مارون ۳)

sron_20260608_38.51N_54.79E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The 56 t/hr methane plume detected by TROPOMI on 8 June 2026 is most consistent with associated gas venting or flaring from the Bugdaýly oil field in Turkmenistan's Gograndag-Okarem petroleum province. The detection sits in the Bugdaýly geňeşligi administrative area, and wind from the west (280°) places the likely source 2–10 km upwind, toward mapped power infrastructure and railway corridors that serve oil production in this remote part of Balkan Region. Twenty previous TROPOMI detections within 30 km since 2023 — all in the 43,000–116,000 kg/hr range — confirm a persistent, large-scale methane source characteristic of the uncontrolled venting of associated gas from oil extraction that has made Turkmenistan the world's most intense methane super-emitter. The exact well pad or processing facility cannot be identified from available inventories, as neither OGIM nor OpenStreetMap map individual oil and gas infrastructure in this area, but the Bugdaýly field is listed among the major onshore oil fields operated by the state company Türkmennebit.

sron_20260608_39.45N_53.72E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Oil and gas production infrastructure in the Goturdepe Oil Field is the likely source of this massive methane plume. Wind on the detection date blew from NNW, and a tight cluster of 12 high-resolution satellite detections (Tanager, EMIT, GHGSat, EnMAP) spanning 2021–2026 pinpoints a persistent emitting source at 39.460°N, 53.715°E — approximately 1.2 km NNW of the TROPOMI pixel centre, directly upwind. The same area has produced TROPOMI detections of 50,000–185,000 kg/hr at least ten times since 2023, making it one of the most persistently observed methane hotspots in Central Asia. The Goturdepe field, operated by Turkmenistan's state oil company Türkmennebit, was identified in a 2023 Guardian investigation as one of the world's largest methane-emitting oil fields, with researchers documenting widespread venting from unlit flares.
sron_20260608_39.45N_53.72E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Goturdepe Oil Field production infrastructure, western Turkmenistan

sron_20260609_36.55N_61.67E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Gas infrastructure in the Dovletabat-Donmez field is the likely source of this 35,000 kg/hr TROPOMI plume. With wind from the north at 4 m/s, the expected source location 2–10 km upwind places it at a fenced industrial compound mapped by OpenStreetMap at 36.58°N, 61.66°E — approximately 3.4 km north-northwest of the detection coordinate. The site lies within one of Turkmenistan's largest gas fields, operated by the state company Turkmengas, and the area has a dense 199-detection history spanning multiple years and sensors, with rates reaching 82,000 kg/hr, consistent with persistent, large-volume methane releases from gas production and processing. No high-resolution sensor has pinpointed this specific compound, but the wind, proximity, industrial land use, and the field's documented status as one of the world's most prolific methane-emitting regions together make it the strongest candidate.
sron_20260609_36.55N_61.67E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Dovletabat-Donmez gas field infrastructure, Mary Region, Turkmenistan

sron_20260609_36.75N_9.93E|SRON_Weekly_M.paragraph: The Borj Chakir landfill, Tunisia's largest controlled landfill serving Greater Tunis, is the likely source of this 7,000 kg/hr TROPOMI methane plume detected on 9 June 2026. The detection coordinate lies ~12.7 km WNW of the landfill, consistent with the SE→NW wind (1.4 m/s) that would carry emissions downwind into the TROPOMI pixel. The attribution is strongly supported by an exceptional detection history: over 30 high-resolution observations from Carbon Mapper, GHGSat, and EMIT between 2023 and 2026 all cluster precisely on this landfill, with IMEO consistently classifying them as waste-sector emissions. Rates from these sensors range from ~800 to nearly 7,000 kg/hr, confirming a large, persistent methane source characteristic of a major municipal solid waste landfill.

sron_20260609_38.29N_53.83E|SRON_Weekly_.operator: DEA Deutsche Erdoel AG (Harbour Energy Group)
sron_20260609_38.29N_53.83E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Offshore oil and gas production infrastructure in Turkmenistan's TM Block 23 in the South Caspian Basin is the likely source of this plume. The 188,000 kg/hr TROPOMI detection on 9 June 2026 sits within this licence area, with NNW winds placing the source 2–10 km further offshore. The area has a dense detection history — 37 TROPOMI plumes over two years at rates from 17,000 to 339,000 kg/hr, plus three high-resolution detections (Landsat-8, EMIT, and EnMAP) clustered at a specific point 16.5 km ENE — confirming persistent, massive methane emissions consistent with chronic venting or flaring inefficiency at offshore production platforms. The licence is held by DEA Deutsche Erdoel AG, part of the Harbour Energy group, though specific platform names could not be confirmed from available data.
sron_20260609_38.29N_53.83E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Offshore oil and gas infrastructure in Caspian Sea

sron_20260609_39.51N_53.21E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Offshore oil and gas production platforms in Turkmenistan's Cheleken Contract Area are the likely source of this massive methane plume. The TROPOMI detection at 39.51°N, 53.21°E sits in the Caspian Sea, and with wind from the north, the source lies upwind — approximately 5–6 km north, around 39.56°N, 53.22°E, where 11 other TROPOMI detections between 2023 and 2026 form a tight cluster with rates of 74,000–275,000 kg/hr. The location coincides with the Cheleken oil accumulation (MapStand) in the South Caspian Basin, where Dragon Oil, a subsidiary of ENOC, operates the Lam and Zhdanov offshore fields. All mapped onshore infrastructure (Dragon Oil pumping stations, flares, petroleum terminals) lies 11–14 km to the south and is outside the upwind search zone, leaving the offshore platforms as the only plausible candidate for a persistent emission of this magnitude.
sron_20260609_39.51N_53.21E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Dragon Oil offshore platforms, Cheleken field, Caspian Sea
sron_20260609_39.51N_53.21E|SRON_Weekly_.source_name: Dragon Oil Cheleken Contract Area offshore production platforms (Lam/Zhdanov fields)

sron_20260610_23.01N_72.63E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The Pirana Municipal Landfill, 7.2 km WSW of the TROPOMI detection, is the most likely source. Surface wind on 10 June 2026 was from the SW at 3.2 m/s, placing the landfill squarely upwind — the plume detected at 23.01°N, 72.63°E lies 63° NE of the landfill, closely matching the wind direction. Nine high-resolution satellite detections from Carbon Mapper's Tanager, ISS, PRISMA, and EMIT instruments between 2023 and 2026 pinpoint the landfill itself as a persistent methane emitter, with rates of 950–4,000 kg/hr at the source. The TROPOMI-measured rate of 16,000 kg/hr (typical range 9,000–23,000 kg/hr) is consistent with a major municipal solid waste disposal site, and no oil and gas infrastructure or coal mines exist in the upwind quadrant.

sron_20260611_31.18N_48.73E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Oil and gas infrastructure within the Namavaran oil field in Iran's Khuzestan province is the likely source of this methane plume. The TROPOMI detection on 11 June 2026 (41,000 kg/hr) sits 6.2 km downwind of a location at 31.163°N, 48.667°E where the higher-resolution Carbon Mapper (Tanager) instrument detected methane on three separate occasions between November 2025 and March 2026, with rates of 405–918 kg/hr. The site lies within the Namavaran producing oil accumulation (MapStand), discovered in 2019, and the wider area has registered 199 TROPOMI detections since late 2023 — one of the most persistently observed methane sources in the region — with rates reaching as high as 77,000 kg/hr. The precise Carbon Mapper coordinates point to a well pad or gathering facility, but the specific installation is not identified in available OpenStreetMap or OGIM infrastructure inventories.

sron_20260611_37.46N_60.65E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Gas pipeline infrastructure operated by the state company Türkmengaz in the desert northeast of Tejen, Turkmenistan, is the most likely source of this 47,000 kg/hr methane plume. The TROPOMI detection at 37.46°N, 60.65°E sits downwind of a known persistent emission cluster at approximately 37.52°N, 60.71°E — 8.5 km to the northeast, closely aligned with the NE wind (from 43°) on 11 June 2026 that would carry the plume toward the detection coordinate. That upwind location has previously produced TROPOMI plumes of 100,000–156,000 kg/hr classified by IMEO as oil-and-gas sector emissions, and operational gas pipelines of the Turkmenistan gas transmission system cross the area. Neither OGIM nor OpenStreetMap record any mapped facilities at this location, which is typical of Turkmenistan's opaque gas sector, but the emission scale is consistent with a compressor station or gas-gathering infrastructure venting. Some 48 satellite methane detections have been recorded within 30 km, confirming this stretch of the Amu-Darya Basin as a persistent super-emitting region.
sron_20260611_37.46N_60.65E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Turkmenistan gas pipeline infrastructure northeast of Tejen

sron_20260611_37.74N_53.83E|SRON_Weekly_.operator: DEA Deutsche Erdoel AG (Harbour Energy Group)
sron_20260611_37.74N_53.83E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Oil and gas production or processing infrastructure in the western portion of TM Block 23 is the likely source of this methane plume. The TROPOMI detection on 11 June 2026 at 37.74°N, 53.83°E, with daily-mean wind from the WSW, places the source 2–10 km upwind — near the Caspian Sea coast at approximately 37.72–73°N, 53.75–80°E. The observed emission rate of 39,000 kg/hr is consistent with large-scale gas venting or flaring from hydrocarbon operations. The area sits within the TM Block 23 licence (operator: DEA Deutsche Erdoel AG / Harbour Energy Group) and has a dense 199-detection history spanning 2023–2026, confirming persistent super-emitter activity across this section of the South Caspian Basin. A separate high-resolution Carbon Mapper cluster 8 km ENE at gas storage tanks (OSM node/9383757860) confirms at least one other methane source in the immediate area, but wind geometry rules it out as the origin of this particular plume. The specific facility at the upwind location could not be identified from available mapping data; higher-resolution imagery would be needed to pinpoint the exact equipment.
sron_20260611_37.74N_53.83E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Oil and gas infrastructure, TM Block 23, Turkmenistan

sron_20260611_58.08N_106.35E|SRON_Weekly.paragraph: The Yarakta oil and gas condensate field's central processing complex in Irkutsk Oblast is the likely source of this 26 t/hr TROPOMI methane plume. Wind from the ENE on the detection date places the source upwind of the reported coordinate, precisely where 18 high-resolution Carbon Mapper (Tanager) detections have repeatedly observed plumes — at rates from 390 to over 10,000 kg/hr — clustered tightly around the field's gas treatment, compression, storage, and flare infrastructure at 58.09°N, 106.57°E, approximately 13 km east of the TROPOMI pixel. The field is the primary asset of Irkutsk Oil Company (INK), accounting for roughly 80% of its hydrocarbon production, and OpenStreetMap maps an integrated gas processing unit (УКПГ), dozens of gasometers, multiple flares, and a central oil and gas treatment facility (ДНС ЦППНГ) at the detection cluster. The persistent, multi-sensor detection record over more than 18 months confirms a major, ongoing emission source at this complex.
sron_20260611_58.08N_106.35E|SRON_Weekly.source_label: Yarakta oil and gas field processing complex
sron_20260611_58.08N_106.35E|SRON_Weekly.source_name: Yarakta Oil and Gas Condensate Field (Ярактинское НГКМ)

sron_20260612_30.84N_49.63E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Oil and gas infrastructure in the north-western sector of Iran's Agha Jari oil field is the likely source of this 108,000 kg/hr methane plume. The wind on 12 June 2026 was from the north-west (310°) at 4.3 m/s, and the plume coordinate sits almost exactly downwind of a location at approximately 30.93°N, 49.52°E — the same area where TROPOMI detected large plumes of 34,000 and 41,000 kg/hr in February 2026 and December 2023 respectively. The Agha Jari field, a supergiant oil accumulation producing since 1936 and spanning 268 km², contains extensive gas-oil separation and handling infrastructure operated by the National Iranian South Oil Company, though the specific facility responsible could not be identified from available mapping. The emission rate, the largest ever detected by satellite in this area, suggests a major operational event such as a flare upset, process venting, or gas blowdown rather than routine emissions.
sron_20260612_30.84N_49.63E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Agha Jari oil field gas infrastructure, NW Khuzestan

sron_20260612_37.68N_61.51E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Natural gas production infrastructure operated by Turkmengaz is the most likely source of this massive methane plume, detected at 111,000 kg/hr on 12 June 2026 by TROPOMI. The detection sits within a dense cluster of 147 satellite observations recorded over three years across a ~25 km area of Turkmenistan's Amu Darya basin, with rates reaching 483,000 kg/hr — among the largest methane plumes observed globally. Wind from the NNE on the detection day places the probable source roughly 8–10 km upwind of the reported coordinate, in an area where well pads and gathering infrastructure are not publicly mapped. The Turkmengaz Drilling Production Base (OSM way 835121754) lies 10 km southeast and anchors the broader emission hotspot, though the specific emitting equipment responsible for this plume cannot be identified from available data.
sron_20260612_37.68N_61.51E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Turkmengaz gas production in Amu Darya basin

sron_20260612_37.99N_53.79E|SRON_Weekly_.operator: DEA Deutsche Erdoel AG (Harbour Energy group)
sron_20260612_37.99N_53.79E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Offshore oil and gas production platforms in Turkmenistan's TM Block 23 in the Caspian Sea are the likely source of this 113,000 kg/hr methane plume. The TROPOMI detection at 37.99°N, 53.79°E sits just offshore, and the wind on 12 June 2026 was from the WNW at 4.6 m/s, placing the source 2–10 km upwind — further into the Caspian, within the TM Block 23 licence area operated by DEA Deutsche Erdoel AG (Harbour Energy group). The area has produced 199 satellite methane detections between April 2024 and June 2026, with TROPOMI rates reaching 160,000 kg/hr, indicating massive, persistent venting or fugitive emissions from offshore production. Carbon Mapper high-resolution detections also confirm persistent sources at specific onshore and nearshore locations to the east. The enormous aggregated emission rates and multi-year persistence are consistent with ongoing offshore oil and gas operations rather than a transient event.
sron_20260612_37.99N_53.79E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Offshore platforms, TM Block 23, Caspian Sea

sron_20260612_38.57N_54.28E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Oil and gas production infrastructure in the Korpeje (Körpeje) field is the likely source of this large methane plume. The TROPOMI detection on 12 June 2026 measured 87,000 kg/hr at 38.57°N, 54.28°E, and 32 high-resolution detections from Carbon Mapper, IMEO/PRISMA, EMIT, and EnMAP consistently pinpoint two persistent emission clusters 1.5–2.4 km NNE of the TROPOMI coordinate at approximately 38.582°N, 54.286°E and 38.588°N, 54.294°E — both within the Korpeje field boundary. These clusters have been detected repeatedly from February 2023 through May 2026 at rates of 200–2,300 kg/hr, with the TROPOMI pixel's 5.5×7 km footprint capturing cumulative emissions from the broader field. The Korpeje field, discovered in 1995 and operated by Turkmenistan's state oil company Türkmennebit, supplies the Korpeje–Kordkuy gas pipeline to Iran; the surface infrastructure at the emission coordinates is not mapped in OpenStreetMap, consistent with the limited public mapping of Turkmenistan's energy infrastructure.
sron_20260612_38.57N_54.28E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Korpeje oil and gas field infrastructure

The sheer scale and multi-year persistence point to field-wide associated gas venting rather than an isolated equipment failure.

sron_20260613_62.51N_66.06E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The Oktyabrskaya compressor station (KC 1-8), operated by Gazprom Transgaz Yugorsk, is the most likely source of this 83,000 kg/hr methane plume, though the wind alignment is imperfect. No other mapped infrastructure within the 15 km search radius — including two small landfills and oil terminals — approaches the scale needed to produce an emission of this magnitude. A previous TROPOMI detection in September 2023 recorded an 11,000 kg/hr plume 7.9 km to the north, suggesting a persistent gas-infrastructure source in the corridor of major Gazprom trunklines (Urengoy–Uzhgorod, Yamburg–Elets) that traverse this part of the West Siberian Basin.
sron_20260613_62.51N_66.06E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Oktyabrskaya compressor station, Gazprom Transgaz Yugorsk

sron_20260613_67.45N_63.92E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Methane ventilation from the Zapolyarnaya and Vorkutinskaya underground coal mines is the likely source of this 18 t/hr TROPOMI plume, detected on 13 June 2026 near Vorkuta, Russia. The combined emissions from these shafts — all operated by Vorkutaugol — can account for the observed rate, and the area's 81 prior satellite detections, uniformly classified as coal-related, leave little doubt that the Vorkuta basin's underground mine ventilation is the responsible source.

sron_20260613_67.49N_64.04E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The Vorkutinskaya underground coal mine is the likely source of this 14,000 kg/hr methane plume detected by TROPOMI on 13 June 2026. The mine's ventilation shaft, mapped 3.8 km WNW of the detection coordinate, has been repeatedly detected by Carbon Mapper's Tanager satellite — six high-resolution observations between April 2025 and May 2026 cluster directly on the shaft at rates of 765–4,931 kg/hr, confirming it as a persistent methane emitter. The TROPOMI detection sits within the sensor's 5.5×7 km pixel footprint over the Vorkuta coal basin, where 81 satellite detections from TROPOMI, Tanager, and PRISMA across the archive — the overwhelming majority classified as coal-sector — make this one of the most consistently observed methane hotspot regions globally. Near-calm winds (0.1 m/s from the ESE) on the detection day mean minimal plume drift, consistent with the mine complex as the emission origin.

sron_20260614_38.26N_53.97E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: A gas production or processing facility in the Korpedzhe (Korpeje) gas field in western Turkmenistan is the likely source of this plume. Emissions at the site have been observed at rates between 800 and 8,600 kg/hr across 17 months (January 2025–June 2026) and are consistent with ongoing gas production operations. The Korpedzhe field is a major onshore gas field operated by the state-owned Turkmengas State Concern and feeds the Korpeje–Kordkuy pipeline to Iran. The specific facility (well pad, gathering station, or compressor) cannot be identified from available mapping data, as neither OGIM nor OpenStreetMap catalogues infrastructure at this coordinate.
sron_20260614_38.26N_53.97E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Gas infrastructure in Turkmenistan's Korpedzhe (Korpeje) gas field

sron_20260614_38.68N_54.30E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The 33,000 kg/hr TROPOMI plume detected on 14 June 2026 is most consistent with emissions from the Ekizak oil and gas field in Turkmenistan's Balkan Region. An OSM-mapped flare (node 12571261803) sits at the centre of the largest cluster in the detection history — 33 high-resolution detections by Tanager, EMIT, PRISMA, Sentinel-2 and Landsat 8 between 2021 and 2026, with rates reaching 11,400 kg/hr — leaving little doubt about the source location. Wind on the detection date was from the north-west at 2.8 m/s, and while the TROPOMI pixel centre lies 1.4 km west of the flare, the 5.5×7 km pixel integrates the entire field. The Ekizak accumulation is a producing gas-and-oil field operated by Türkmennebit, the Turkmen state oil company whose western fields were identified by the Guardian in 2023 as the world's worst methane super-emitter, with extinguished flares and widespread venting.
sron_20260614_38.68N_54.30E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Ekizak oil field flare and infrastructure, western Turkmenistan

sron_20260614_39.43N_53.53E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Oil and gas production infrastructure in the Koturdepe (Goturdepe) field is the likely source of this 102,000 kg/hr TROPOMI methane plume detected on 14 June 2026 near Balkanabat, Turkmenistan. A second persistent cluster 3.5–4.3 km ENE adds further evidence of widespread chronic emissions from this mature onshore oil and gas field, which lies within the MapStand-mapped Koturtepe accumulation in the South Caspian Basin. The TROPOMI pixel likely integrates methane from multiple sources across the field; no specific well pad or facility is mapped in OpenStreetMap at the primary upwind cluster coordinates.
sron_20260614_39.43N_53.53E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Koturdepe oil and gas field, Turkmenistan

sron_20260614_64.06N_68.81E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The methane plume is most consistent with a release from unmapped oil and gas infrastructure in the remote West Siberian taiga. sron_20260615_39.29N_62.56E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Gas production infrastructure within the Bagaja gas discovery area in Turkmenistan's Amu-Darya Basin is the most likely source of this 79,000 kg/hr methane plume. sron_20260615_39.94N_63.05E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The 115 t/hr methane plume detected by TROPOMI on 15 June 2026 at 39.94°N, 63.05°E in Uzbekistan's Karakul District is most consistent with a major emission from unmapped gas production infrastructure in the Amu-Darya Basin. sron_20260615_64.77N_72.39E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: A ~27,000 kg/hr methane plume detected by TROPOMI on 15 June 2026 at 64.77°N, 72.39°E in the Nadymsky Rayon of Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug cannot be confidently attributed to a specific source. Two TROPOMI detections from June 2024 recorded a similar ~26,000 kg/hr plume 5.5 km southwest of the current detection, confirming a persistent large source classified by IMEO as oil-and-gas related. The true source may be an unmapped well pad or pipeline facility within the SLKH 02,520 HP licence area or along the SRTO-Ural pipeline corridor, but available evidence does not single out a specific facility.

sron_20260616_32.22N_103.56W|SRON_Weekly.paragraph: The 16,000 kg/hr TROPOMI methane plume detected on 16 June 2026 is most consistent with aggregate emissions from the dense oil and gas production infrastructure in this section of New Mexico's Delaware Basin. sron_20260616_45.64S_68.51W|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The 62,000 kg/hr TROPOMI methane detection is most consistent with aggregate emissions from the Rio Chico production area of the Cerro Dragón oil field, operated by Pan American Energy in Chubut, Argentina. sron_20260617_23.68S_46.59W|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The 21,000 kg/hr TROPOMI methane plume detected on 17 June 2026 is most consistent with emissions from the Aterro Sanitário de Santo André (Santo André municipal landfill), located 10.6 km almost due east of the plume coordinate — a near-perfect alignment with the easterly wind that day. A second landfill, Lara Central de Tratamento de Resíduos, sits 3.7 km to the south and also shows frequent high-resolution methane detections (1,000–5,500 kg/hr); given TROPOMI's 5.5×7 km pixel, both landfills likely contribute to the integrated signal. The area has registered 76 satellite methane detections from four different sensors since 2023, confirming it as one of South America's most persistent landfill methane hotspots.

sron_20260617_31.09N_49.75E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Oil and gas production infrastructure within the Karanj oil field is the most likely source of this 23,000 kg/hr methane plume. The large emission rate and location within an active oil field with gas injection and associated flaring support this attribution, though the TROPOMI pixel size prevents pinpointing a specific facility.

sron_20260617_31.64N_102.08W|SRON_Weekly.paragraph: The TROPOMI plume detected on 17 June 2026 is most consistent with a persistent methane super-emitter located approximately 2.2 km south-southwest of the reported coordinate at 31.6205°N, 102.0833°W. This location has been detected five times since 2023 by high-resolution sensors — including Carbon Mapper's Global Airborne Observatory and NASA's EMIT instrument — at rates of 1,200 to 3,300 kg per hour, making it the most active and repeatedly confirmed emission source in the immediate area. The site sits almost directly upwind of the TROPOMI coordinate under the prevailing southerly wind (197°, 4.9 m/s), with a bearing alignment error of only 7°. Although the specific infrastructure is not catalogued in the OGIM or OpenStreetMap databases, the location falls within OVINTIV USA Inc.'s Davidson lease, whose nearest active well (Davidson '46C' #7) is 0.9 km away. The elevated TROPOMI rate of 20,000 kg/hr, several times larger than any previous single-sensor detection at this site, likely reflects the integration of emissions from this persistent source together with other nearby well pads and facilities — including COG Operating LLC's Windham TXL wells 2 km to the west-southwest — within TROPOMI's 5.5 × 7 km footprint.

sron_20260617_33.33N_7.32W|SRON_Weekly_M.paragraph: The Décharge de Médiouna, Casablanca's main municipal landfill, is the most likely source of this methane plume. The wind on the detection date was from the northwest at 308°, and the landfill lies approximately 30 km upwind — a near-perfect alignment with only 4° angular offset. Seven high-resolution Carbon Mapper detections between 2024 and 2026 pinpoint the landfill itself at rates of 2,400–8,600 kg/hr, while 58 TROPOMI detections from 2023–2026, all classified as waste-sector by UN IMEO, form a persistent downwind trail consistent with a single dominant super-emitter. Although 30 km exceeds TROPOMI's typical 2–10 km source offset, the landfill's scale — serving the Casablanca metropolitan area of over four million people — and the tight clustering of Carbon Mapper observations directly on the facility make it the only credible mapped source in the region.

The site sits in the Korpeje gas field, operated by Turkmenistan's state oil company Türkmennebit, with mapped gasometers and storage tanks 3.8 km to the NNW confirming active gas infrastructure in the immediate vicinity. sron_20260617_54.00N_87.37E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The Yerunakovskaya coal mining complex in Russia's Kuznetsk Basin is the likely source of this 38,000 kg/hr methane plume. Surface wind on the detection date was from the NNE at 2.2 m/s, placing the source 2–10 km NNE of the TROPOMI coordinate — directly toward the Yerunakovsky open pit (10 km NNE) and the Yerunakovskaya-8 underground coal mine (13.6 km N, operated by Raspadskaya/Evraz, producing 2.3 Mt/yr).
