The broader area has 199 satellite methane detections in the 30-km archive, overwhelmingly classified as coal, and high-resolution Carbon Mapper (Tanager) observations have pinpointed coal-related methane vents at multiple locations across the mining district. The TROPOMI sensor's 5.5×7 km footprint prevents attribution to a single ventilation shaft, but the wind direction, emission rate, and detection history are all consistent with underground coal mine ventilation from the Yerunakovskaya complex.
sron_20260617_54.00N_87.37E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Yerunakovskaya coal mining complex, Kuznetsk Basin

sron_20260617_54.58N_83.46E|SRON_Weekly_.evidence_note: Web search tools were unavailable; evidence URLs are from the context.json coal_mines and osm fields (Global Coal Mine Tracker and OpenStreetMap).
sron_20260617_54.58N_83.46E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The Vostochny Coal Mine (Eastern section of the Kolyvansky open-pit), part of the Siberian Anthracite group, is the likely source of this 31,000 kg/hr methane plume. The TROPOMI detection sits 13 km downwind (southwest) of the mine, with surface wind from the northeast aligning the plume to within 4° of the mine bearing. Three high-resolution Carbon Mapper (Tanager) detections in 2025–2026 pinpoint methane emissions within 700 m of the Vostochny mine pit and are classified as coal-sector sources by IMEO. The broader detection history includes 19 TROPOMI detections in the NE upwind sector since 2023 at rates of 5,000–24,000 kg/hr, confirming a persistent, large-scale coal mine methane source from this anthracite mining complex.
sron_20260617_54.58N_83.46E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Vostochny coal mine, Siberian Anthracite complex, Novosibirsk
sron_20260617_54.58N_83.46E|SRON_Weekly_.source_name: Vostochny Coal Mine (Восточный участок Колыванского разреза)

evidence: https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Чулымский_район (notes oil and gas pipelines crossing the district and extensive peat deposits)
sron_20260617_55.51N_81.90E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: No anthropogenic methane source could be identified for this 29,000 kg/hr TROPOMI plume detected on 17 June 2026 in Chulymsky District, Novosibirsk Oblast. The detection coordinate (55.51°N, 81.90°E) and its upwind search area (2–10 km ENE, per the daily wind from 62°) contain no mapped oil and gas infrastructure, coal mines, landfills, or industrial facilities in OGIM, OpenStreetMap, MapStand, or the Global Coal Mine Tracker. The nearest mapped gas pipeline — the Omsk–Novosibirsk trunkline operated by Gazprom Transgaz Tomsk — lies 41 km to the south, well outside the sensor's source-attribution horizon. The area sits within the Baraba Lowland, a vast wetland and peat-bog complex; two similarly large TROPOMI plumes (8,000–9,000 kg/hr) were detected 28 km to the SSW in June 2024, consistent with a recurring seasonal pattern of high wetland methane emissions during the spring thaw. However, the exceptionally high emission rate and the absence of detailed wetland-flux ground-truthing mean an unmapped anthropogenic source cannot be entirely excluded.
sron_20260617_55.51N_81.90E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Unidentified source in Baraba Lowland wetlands

sron_20260617_64.29N_69.15E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The Sorumska compressor station (KC 5–7), 8 km south-southwest of the TROPOMI detection, is the most plausible source of this 40,000 kg/hr methane plume. Operated by Gazprom Transgaz Yugorsk, the station has 467 MW of installed compressor capacity across seven workshops servicing trunk gas pipelines from West Siberian fields — the only infrastructure in the area capable of emissions at this scale. Three other large TROPOMI plumes (18,000–97,000 kg/hr) have been detected in the vicinity since 2023, one classified by IMEO as an oil and gas source, consistent with recurrent operational venting or blowdowns at the compressor station. However, the daily-mean wind is from the southeast while the station lies to the south-southwest — a 75° offset from the expected upwind direction — so the attribution relies on the station being the sole facility of sufficient scale within the search radius, with the caveat that actual wind at the satellite overpass may have differed from the daily mean.
sron_20260617_64.29N_69.15E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Sorumska gas compressor station, Gazprom Transgaz Yugorsk

sron_20260618_25.52N_99.73W|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The most likely source is an unmapped facility approximately 1.6 km SSE of the TROPOMI detection coordinate (25.51°N, 99.72°W), near the village of Pueblo Nuevo in Cadereyta Jiménez municipality. Wind on the detection date was from the SSE at 1.7 m/s, placing the source directly upwind of the plume. Three TROPOMI detections clustered within 3.5 km of each other over 2.5 years (13,000–18,000 kg/hr) indicate a persistent high-rate emitter. The UN IMEO system classified the closest historical detection (2024-12-26, 3.5 km away) as a waste-sector source, but no landfill, wastewater plant, or active gas infrastructure is mapped in OpenStreetMap or the OGIM inventory at the estimated source location. The Burgos Basin gas province underlies the area, so unmapped oil and gas infrastructure cannot be ruled out. Without higher-resolution imagery or ground validation, the specific facility remains unidentified.
sron_20260618_25.52N_99.73W|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Unmapped landfill or gas infrastructure near Pueblo Nuevo

sron_20260618_37.76N_53.84E|SRON_Weekly_.operator: Harbour Energy PLC / DEA Deutsche Erdoel AG
sron_20260618_37.76N_53.84E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: An onshore gas processing and storage facility on Turkmenistan's Caspian coast is the most likely source of this 109,000 kg/hr TROPOMI methane plume, detected on 18 June 2026. The facility — mapped in OpenStreetMap with gasometers, storage tanks, a chimney, and process buildings — sits within the TM Block 23 licence area operated by Harbour Energy/DEA. Over 190 satellite detections since 2023 confirm this as an extraordinarily persistent methane hotspot, with high-resolution sensors (Carbon Mapper Tanager and ISS, EMIT, Sentinel-2, and Landsat 8) repeatedly pinpointing emissions at the facility. The TROPOMI detection coordinate lies 6.7 km west of the facility; while the daily-mean wind was WNW (which would place the source upwind, in the opposite direction), coastal sea-breeze reversals or TROPOMI's 5.5×7 km pixel gridding may explain the offset — no infrastructure is mapped in the upwind search corridor.
sron_20260618_37.76N_53.84E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: TM Block 23 onshore gas facility, Caspian coast

sron_20260618_65.21N_78.40E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Oil and gas production infrastructure in the Vostochno-Tarkosalinskoe (East Tarkosalinskoye) field is the likely source of this 73,000 kg/hr methane plume detected by TROPOMI on 18 June 2026. The wind was from the south, placing the source 2–10 km upwind of the detection coordinate — directly within this large producing oil, gas and condensate field operated by NOVATEK-TARKOSALENEFT OOO (a NOVATEK subsidiary). TROPOMI has detected persistent large methane emissions from this field in three consecutive summers (22,000 kg/hr in July 2024, 31,000 kg/hr in June 2025, and now 73,000 kg/hr in June 2026), indicating a recurring and possibly worsening emissions problem. The specific facility within the field cannot be pinpointed from available data, though MapStand records confirm multiple wellheads in the upwind corridor, including East Tarkosalinskoye well 900 located 6.9 km directly south of the detection.
sron_20260618_65.21N_78.40E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: East Tarkosalinskoye oil and gas field

sron_20260618_65.63N_79.09E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Gas production operations in the Beregovoye field are the likely source of this 70 t/hr methane plume. The TROPOMI detection sits within the Beregovoye licence area (SLKH 02,532 HP) in Russia's Yamalo-Nenets region, a major onshore gas field operated by Sibneftegaz with recoverable reserves of 324 billion m³. Surface winds were from the south at 3.6 m/s, placing the probable source 2–10 km upwind — well within the field's 1,754 km² licence boundary where no other industrial infrastructure is mapped. The emission rate is consistent with venting or incomplete flaring during gas production operations, though the absence of repeat detections in the satellite record suggests an intermittent event such as a maintenance blowdown rather than persistent leakage.
sron_20260618_65.63N_79.09E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Beregovoye gas field operations, West Siberia

sron_20260619_37.79N_53.96E|SRON_Weekly_.operator: DEA Deutsche Erdoel AG (Harbour Energy PLC)
sron_20260619_37.79N_53.96E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: A gas processing and storage facility in the Keimir (Keymir) gas field of western Turkmenistan is the likely source of this 49,000 kg/hr TROPOMI methane plume detected on 19 June 2026. The TROPOMI pixel is centred 4.1 km downwind (ENE) of the facility, consistent with the westerly wind (262°) that day, and exactly matching the expected 2–10 km source offset for this sensor. A dense cluster of 26 high-resolution detections from Carbon Mapper's Tanager, EMIT, EnMAP and ISS instruments — spanning August 2022 to June 2026 — pinpoints persistent methane emissions from the gas infrastructure at this location, where OpenStreetMap maps two gasometers, three storage tanks and a chimney. The facility sits within the Keimir gas accumulation of TM Block 23, operated by DEA Deutsche Erdoel AG (part of the Harbour Energy group), in a country that Wikipedia notes 'possesses the world's fifth-largest reserves of natural gas, and many leaks' and where 'in 2025 most of the world's largest leaks of methane' originated.
sron_20260619_37.79N_53.96E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Keimir gas field processing and storage facility, Turkmenistan

sron_20260619_39.04N_53.88E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Oil and gas production infrastructure in the Korpeje–Goturdepe–Barsagelmez field complex of western Turkmenistan is the most likely source of this enormous 78,000 kg/hr methane plume. The detection sits within the South Caspian Basin's onshore oil and gas belt, a region documented by satellite researchers as one of the world's largest and most persistent methane hotspots, where extinguished flare stacks routinely vent methane directly to the atmosphere. Wind from the east on the detection date places the source roughly 2–10 km east of the TROPOMI pixel centre, within the Block 21 licence area. The 50 prior satellite detections within 30 km, including precise Sentinel-2 and Landsat identifications of persistent point sources, confirm that this stretch of the Caspian coastal plain hosts numerous high-emitting oil and gas facilities, though individual well pads and compressor stations are not mapped in open infrastructure databases.
sron_20260619_39.04N_53.88E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Western Turkmenistan oil and gas field venting

sron_20260619_44.96N_8.55E|SRON_Weekly_M.paragraph: The Discarica ARAL (Castelceriolo landfill), operated by ARAL, is the most likely source of this 9,000 kg/hr methane plume. The landfill sits 4.1 km southwest of the TROPOMI detection coordinate — directly upwind given the southwesterly wind (223°) on 19 June 2026, placing it well within the 2–10 km offset typical for TROPOMI plumes. A 9,000 kg/hr emission rate is consistent with a large municipal waste landfill, and the site has a documented history of fires and subsurface pollution incidents reported by ARPA Piemonte, indicating active methane generation. No other upwind candidate — industrial facilities, biogas digesters, or the unnamed landfill 9 km west — matches the combination of proximity, wind alignment, facility type, and emission scale as well as Discarica ARAL.

sron_20260619_61.02N_76.77E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The TROPOMI detection at 123,000 kg/hr over the Samotlor oil field is most consistent with methane emissions from the densely developed oil and gas infrastructure operated by Samotlorneftegaz AO (Rosneft). The wind on 19 June 2026 blew from the south at 3.1 m/s, placing the likely source area 2–10 km upwind of the plume centroid, where well pads (Куст 1235, 204, 4119, among others) and an unnamed industrial works at 4.5 km SSE saturate the landscape. Carbon Mapper (Tanager) detected persistent plumes of 1,000–3,600 kg/hr from the DNS-27 and DNS-28 booster pump stations 7–9 km NNE of the TROPOMI coordinate earlier in 2026, confirming that gas-handling infrastructure in this sector of the field routinely emits methane, though at rates far below the TROPOMI measurement. The exceptional 123 t/hr rate suggests either a major operational event (blowdown, emergency venting) or the aggregate of numerous sources within the coarse TROPOMI pixel; a specific point source cannot be isolated from the available evidence.
sron_20260619_61.02N_76.77E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Samotlor oil field infrastructure, western Siberia

sron_20260620_37.00N_62.10E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Gas production and processing infrastructure in the southern portion of the Galkynysh gas field is the likely source of this plume. The detection sits within Turkmenistan's Mary Province, home to the world's second-largest gas field, and the 99,000 kg/hr emission rate is consistent with major gas-field operations such as well pads, gathering lines, or compressor stations. Wind from the NNE places the source 2–10 km upwind of the TROPOMI detection, within the southern extent of the Galkynysh field complex. Thirteen prior TROPOMI detections within 30 km — all with similarly large rates between 36,000 and 150,000 kg/hr — confirm persistent, massive methane emissions from this gas field, which is operated by the state company Türkmengaz. The exact facility cannot be pinpointed because TROPOMI's 5.5×7 km pixels and the sparse public infrastructure data for Turkmenistan preclude finer attribution.
sron_20260620_37.00N_62.10E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Galkynysh gas field infrastructure, southern Mary Province

sron_20260620_37.93N_54.31E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: An unnamed fenced industrial compound on the Korpeje–Kordkuy gas pipeline is the most likely source of this 87,000 kg/hr methane plume detected by TROPOMI on 20 June 2026. The compound sits at 37.97°N, 54.27°E — 5.3 km northwest of the reported plume coordinate, closely aligned with the WNW wind direction (284°) that day, placing it in the upwind source zone expected for TROPOMI's 5.5×7 km pixels. The site lies directly on the Korpeje–Kordkuy pipeline (operated by Türkmengaz), and the broader area has produced 64 satellite-detected methane plumes since 2023, with rates reaching 184,000 kg/hr — consistent with chronic, large-scale venting from gas production and transmission infrastructure in western Turkmenistan's South Caspian Basin. The facility's specific function (compressor station, valve station, or gas processing unit) could not be confirmed from available mapping data.
sron_20260620_37.93N_54.31E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Korpeje–Kordkuy gas pipeline facility, western Turkmenistan

sron_20260620_54.03N_85.44E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: A gold mining quarry (Карьер золотодобычи) located 9.2 km NNE of the TROPOMI detection coordinate is the only mapped industrial feature in the upwind direction and is the most plausible candidate, though the attribution is uncertain. A NE wind on the detection day would carry emissions from this quarry toward the plume location, placing it within the expected 2–10 km source offset typical for TROPOMI. A prior large TROPOMI detection (68,000 kg/hr) in May 2023 was recorded 21 km NNE, suggesting a persistent methane source in this mining region at the western edge of the Kuznetsk Basin, but the 2023 plume's relationship to this quarry is unclear. Gold mining is not a typical large methane source, and the 39,000 kg/hr emission rate is more characteristic of coal mine ventilation or gas infrastructure; the quarry may intersect coal-bearing strata or there may be unmapped mining or gas infrastructure nearby that the available databases do not capture.
sron_20260620_54.03N_85.44E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Gold mining quarry northeast of Tyagun station

sron_20260620_54.11N_87.38E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The Yerunakovskaya-8 underground coal mine in Russia's Kuzbass basin is the most likely source of this 42,000 kg/hr methane plume. The mine, operated by Raspadskaya Coal Company (a subsidiary of Evraz), sits 2.1 km northwest of the TROPOMI plume coordinate, and a 43,000 kg/hr TROPOMI detection on 24 June 2026 was located just 1.0 km from the mine — confirming it as a persistent, very large emitter. On this day, a north-easterly wind points to emissions from the mine's eastern ventilation shafts at approximately 54.11°N 87.40°E, where high-resolution Carbon Mapper (Tanager) satellites have repeatedly detected coal-related methane plumes of 300–1,400 kg/hr from individual vents. The area has 199 satellite detections in the archive, with multiple Tanager clusters tracing the mine's ventilation network across a 5 km radius, and the TROPOMI pixel integrates these into the very large plume observed.

sron_20260620_54.16N_82.79E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: An unmapped waste disposal site in the Verkh-Miltyushinsky Selsoviet area (~54.23–54.25°N, 82.85–82.86°E) is the likely source of this 19,000 kg/hr methane plume. The TROPOMI detection sits roughly 9–11 km downwind (SSW) of this area, with a near-perfect match to the daily NNE wind direction (0–10° deviation). Two earlier TROPOMI detections from July 2024, approximately 30 km further downwind along the same NNE–SSW axis, were independently classified as 'waste' by IMEO analysts and show the same wind-consistent geometry from this same source area — strong evidence of a persistent methane-emitting waste site. The emission rate (19,000–32,000 kg/hr across three detections) is consistent with a large, unmanaged landfill lacking gas capture. No named waste facility is mapped in OpenStreetMap at this location; the nearest mapped features are farmyards, and the only mapped landfill in the district sits 13 km east with poor wind alignment (49° off), making it an unlikely source for this plume.
sron_20260620_54.16N_82.79E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Unmapped waste disposal site near Verkh-Miltyushinsky Selsoviet

sron_20260621_22.83S_47.18W|SRON_Weekly_.operator: Empresa de Saneamento e Tratamento de Resíduos (ESTRE)
sron_20260621_22.83S_47.18W|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The ESTRE Paulínia Landfill, approximately 6.5 km NNW of the TROPOMI plume coordinate, is the likely source. Wind from the WNW on the detection day would carry the plume broadly toward the ESE, consistent with the TROPOMI pixel located SSE of the landfill — well within the sensor's coarse 5.5×7 km footprint. The attribution is strongly supported by the detection history: 14 Carbon Mapper and IMEO/EMIT detections between 2023 and 2026 cluster precisely on the landfill polygon (OSM way/625335308), all tagged as waste-sector emissions, with rates ranging from 270 to 5,800 kg/hr — consistent with a large active landfill. The Paulínia Landfill Gas Project, operated by ESTRE, has been a registered CDM project since 2006 with documented methane capture and flaring infrastructure, though the repeated satellite detections indicate fugitive or operational emissions persist.
sron_20260621_22.83S_47.18W|SRON_Weekly_.source_name: Paulínia Landfill (ESTRE Paulínia Landfill Gas Project)

sron_20260621_23.36S_46.76W|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The Aterro Sanitário de Caieiras, operated by Essencis Soluções Ambientais, is the likely source of this 20,000 kg/hr TROPOMI methane plume. The landfill sits 2.1 km northwest of the plume coordinate — directly upwind under the NW wind recorded that day, which would carry emissions SE to the TROPOMI pixel. The attribution is strongly supported by 34 high-resolution detections (Carbon Mapper Tanager, EMIT, and EnMAP) from 2023–2025 that cluster with a centroid just 46 metres from the landfill centre, with rates of 500–5,800 kg/hr typical of a large active landfill. An adjacent landfill gas-to-energy plant (Termoverde Caieiras) confirms active biogas generation at the site, and no other credible methane source exists upwind within the 10 km search horizon.

sron_20260621_31.25N_103.22W|SRON_Weekly.paragraph: The TROPOMI-detected methane plume is most consistent with a source in the Giraffe 18 / Giraffe 4/5 well pad area operated by VTX Energy Operating, LLC, roughly 5.5 km southeast of the reported plume coordinate. The wind on 21 June 2026 was from the southeast, placing this area directly upwind. Two prior TROPOMI overpasses in October 2024 independently placed a 13,000 kg/hr plume within 1.5 km of the same Giraffe 18 permit coordinates, and a Carbon Mapper Tanager detection in March 2026 pinpointed a 518 kg/hr emission just 255 metres from the Giraffe 18 flare permit location. Texas Railroad Commission records show SWR-32 flare permits for this site at rates up to 680,000 mcf per day for system-upset events, and both VIIRS and Sentinel-2 have independently observed active flaring at this location as recently as April–May 2026. The recurring satellite detections at rates spanning three orders of magnitude suggest intermittent but persistent methane releases, likely from flaring, venting, or equipment leaks at this multi-well pad.
sron_20260621_31.25N_103.22W|SRON_Weekly.source_label: VTX Energy Giraffe 18 well pad area, Reeves County

sron_20260621_33.55N_7.45W|SRON_Weekly_M.paragraph: The Décharge de Médiouna, Casablanca's principal municipal landfill, is the near-certain source of this 28,000 kg/hr methane plume. Twenty-one high-resolution satellite detections from Carbon Mapper (Tanager/ISS) and EMIT between 2024 and 2026 repeatedly pinpoint the landfill at approximately 33.478°N, 7.540°W — the centroid of those detections sits just 200 metres from the mapped landfill polygon (OSM way/1362368751). The current TROPOMI detection lies 11.6 km northeast of the landfill; while the daily mean wind was from the WNW, coastal wind variability and TROPOMI's 5.5×7 km pixel resolution can account for the offset. The Médiouna landfill was flagged in a 2025 Nature study as one of the world's most prominent landfill methane hotspots visible from space, receiving an estimated 3,500–6,000 tonnes of Casablanca's waste daily. With 59 satellite detections in the archive — the most of any site in this region — the landfill's emissions are persistent and well-documented.

sron_20260621_36.69N_9.93E|SRON_Weekly_M.paragraph: The Borj Chakir controlled landfill, Greater Tunis's main waste disposal site approximately 14 km ENE of the detection coordinate, is the likely source of this 20,000 kg/hr methane plume. Surface winds on 21 June 2026 were from the ENE at 1.6 m/s, placing the landfill directly upwind of the TROPOMI detection — consistent with the plume drifting WSW from the site. The attribution is reinforced by an exceptional cluster of over 30 satellite detections at this landfill since 2023, recorded by Carbon Mapper, GHGSat, EMIT, and TROPOMI, all classified as waste-sector emissions, with rates ranging from roughly 1,000 to 24,000 kg/hr depending on sensor resolution. An adjacent wastewater treatment plant (ONAS STEP El Attar) may also contribute to the persistent methane signal observed at this location.
sron_20260621_36.69N_9.93E|SRON_Weekly_M.source_name: Borj Chakir Controlled Landfill (Décharge Contrôlée de Borj Chakir)

sron_20260621_50.72N_74.81E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: A large methane plume of 48,000 kg/hr was detected by TROPOMI on 21 June 2026 in Bayanaul District, Pavlodar Region, Kazakhstan, with winds from the NNE placing the likely source 2–10 km north of the reported coordinate. A prior TROPOMI detection at 27,000 kg/hr occurred 24 km north on the same meridian in May 2023, suggesting a persistent but intermittent source. No industrial infrastructure — oil and gas facilities, coal mines, landfills, or mapped industrial sites — appears in any database (OGIM, OSM, Global Coal Mine Tracker) within the search radius; the only mapped features are power transmission towers along the former HVDC Ekibastuz–Centre corridor. The emission rate is consistent with coal mine ventilation or gas infrastructure, but no specific facility could be identified in this remote steppe location.
sron_20260621_50.72N_74.81E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Unidentified source in remote Kazakh steppe

sron_20260621_54.10N_86.98E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The Kyrgayskaya underground coal mine is the likely source of this 57,000 kg/hr methane plume. The mine sits 4.5 km east-northeast of the TROPOMI pixel centre, well within the 2–10 km upwind search zone, and the surface wind on 21 June 2026 was blowing from the northeast — aligning the mine almost directly upwind of the detection. Carbon Mapper (Tanager) has repeatedly imaged methane plumes of 350–770 kg/hr at the mine's ventilation shaft locations, and the Global Energy Monitor wiki documents a dedicated methane plume entry for this facility. With 165 satellite detections clustered across the Kuzbass coalfield within 30 km and this mine being the nearest underground operation in the wind-consistent direction, the ventilation shaft emissions from Kyrgayskaya — an active longwall mine producing 3 million tonnes per year — best account for the observed signal.

sron_20260621_54.55N_86.17E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: A coal mine ventilation drift is the likely source of this 50,000 kg/hr methane plume detected by TROPOMI. The unnamed ventilation drift (OSM way/182705508, 'Вентиляционный штрек') sits 2.7 km northeast of the detection pixel — directly upwind under the day's northeasterly winds — and its plume would drift southwest over the TROPOMI pixel centre. The site lies in Russia's Kuzbass coal basin, one of the world's most methane-intensive mining regions, where 199 satellite detections have been recorded within 30 km. High-resolution Tanager observations confirm persistent methane emissions from multiple mine ventilation and gas-drainage points throughout this corridor, though the specific mine operating this particular drift could not be determined.
sron_20260621_54.55N_86.17E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Coal mine ventilation drift, Kuzbass coal basin
sron_20260621_54.55N_86.17E|SRON_Weekly_.source_name: Unnamed ventilation drift (Вентиляционный штрек) of the Leninsk-Kuznetsky mining complex

sron_20260622_33.36N_7.46W|SRON_Weekly_M.paragraph: The Décharge de Médiouna (Médiouna landfill) is the likely source of this 32,000 kg/hr methane plume. The landfill lies 15 km NNW of the TROPOMI detection coordinate — directly upwind of the plume given the NNW wind — and 12 of 13 high-resolution Carbon Mapper detections from 2024–2026 fall inside the landfill's mapped boundary. The site has registered 63 satellite methane detections since 2023 across TROPOMI, IMEO, and Carbon Mapper sensors, with rates ranging from 1,500 to 53,000 kg/hr, all consistent with a large (~52-hectare) active municipal waste disposal site. Both IMEO and Carbon Mapper independently classify the detections as 'waste' sector.

sron_20260622_33.93N_71.56E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: An unmapped solid waste disposal site on the eastern outskirts of Peshawar, near 34.00°N 71.59°E, is the likely source of this 19,000 kg/hr methane plume detected by TROPOMI on 22 June 2026. The area has lit up 39 times in satellite archives since 2023, with emissions ranging from 11,000 to 41,000 kg/hr — a scale and persistence characteristic of a large landfill serving a major city. UN IMEO's Methane Alert and Response System classifies multiple detections at this cluster as 'waste' sector, and the location sits on the peri-urban fringe of Peshawar (population ~2 million), where municipal solid waste is typically disposed. No specific landfill is mapped in OpenStreetMap at these coordinates, and the Peshawar oil and gas exploration licence held by Hycarpex-American Energy Inc. provides a weaker alternative hypothesis that cannot be ruled out without higher-resolution imagery.
sron_20260622_33.93N_71.56E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Unmapped landfill on Peshawar's eastern outskirts

sron_20260622_35.32N_40.47E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Persistent methane emissions from oil and gas infrastructure at the Jafra oil field in Syria's Euphrates Graben are the likely source of this 5,000 kg/hr TROPOMI plume detected on 22 June 2026. The area has been detected 199 times by multiple satellite archives — including Carbon Mapper, Landsat, Sentinel-2, EMIT, EnMAP, and TROPOMI — between May 2023 and June 2026, with high-resolution sensors pinpointing the source cluster to approximately 35.30°N, 40.46°E, about 2 km south of the TROPOMI plume coordinate and well within TROPOMI's 5.5×7 km pixel footprint. All IMEO-classified detections are tagged as oil and gas, and the cluster sits immediately east of the walled Jafra oil field compound and within the MapStand JAFRA producing oil accumulation. The Syrian Petroleum Company (SPC) is the national operator, with the SPC_AREA licence covering the entire region. Emission rates from high-resolution sensors range from 377 to 5,733 kg/hr, consistent with the current TROPOMI observation, and the multi-year persistence points to routine operational venting or leaking rather than a one-off event.
sron_20260622_35.32N_40.47E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Jafra oil field infrastructure, Deir ez-Zor, Syria

sron_20260622_36.86N_42.09E|SRON_Weekly_.operator: Syrian Petroleum Company / Gulfsands Petroleum PLC (Block 26)
sron_20260622_36.86N_42.09E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The Sweidiyeh gas-fired power station and adjacent refinery complex in Syria's Soueidieh oil field is the most likely source of this plume. Four Carbon Mapper satellite detections between August 2022 and September 2023 — at rates of 792 to 1,404 kg/hr — are clustered directly on this facility (within ~200 m of the power station), confirming it as a persistent methane emitter. The TROPOMI detection on 22 June 2026 reports a larger emission rate of 8,000 kg/hr at a coordinate ~10 km SSW of the complex, a displacement consistent with TROPOMI's 5.5×7 km pixel resolution and the very light wind (0.8 m/s from WNW) on that day. The Sweidiyeh plant was struck by a Turkish airstrike in January 2024 and caught fire, and the wider Soueidieh field — Syria's largest — has seen years of disrupted maintenance and contested operations under Block 26 (Gulfsands Petroleum / Sinochem), making elevated fugitive emissions or unlit flaring plausible. The Rabia landfill 5 km south of the detection coordinate offers a possible alternative but has no satellite detection history, whereas the Sweidiyeh complex is the only facility in the area with repeated, independently confirmed methane plumes.
sron_20260622_36.86N_42.09E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Sweidiyeh gas plant and refinery, Soueidieh oil field
sron_20260622_36.86N_42.09E|SRON_Weekly_.source_name: Sweidiyeh Power Station and adjacent refinery

sron_20260622_40.94N_59.50E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: A large methane plume (61,000 kg/hr, uncertainty ±24,000 kg/hr) was detected by TROPOMI on 22 June 2026 near Şabat District in Turkmenistan's Dashoguz Region. The plume rate and location in Turkmenistan — a country with well-documented massive methane emissions from its oil and gas sector — point to the gas industry as the most likely broad source category. However, no specific facility, well pad, or pipeline infrastructure could be identified: the OGIM inventory, OpenStreetMap, and the Global Coal Mine Tracker all returned no features within the search area, and no prior satellite detections exist within 30 km to guide attribution. Wind from the WSW suggests the source lies 2–10 km upwind of the reported coordinate, but without accessible ground-truth data or web resources for this closed region, a confident attribution to a specific source is not possible.

sron_20260622_57.64N_83.89E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: No specific source could be identified for this 21,000 kg/hr TROPOMI methane plume detected on 22 June 2026 at 57.64°N, 83.89°E in the Molchanovsky District of Tomsk Oblast. The daily-mean wind was from the northeast, placing the likely source 2–10 km upwind (NE) of the reported coordinate, but that area is sparsely populated taiga and swamp with no mapped industrial infrastructure — only two small unnamed buildings and the village of Sulzat 12 km to the NNW. The Nizhnevartovsk–Parabel–Kuzbass gas trunkline (1,020 mm, operated by Gazprom Transgaz Tomsk) and the Molchanovskaya oil pumping station lie 18–22 km to the west and southwest, outside the typical TROPOMI source-offset range. The plume rate and regional setting in the hydrocarbon-rich West Siberian Basin are most consistent with venting or leakage from unmapped gas-production or gathering infrastructure, but the evidence does not single out any candidate.
sron_20260622_57.64N_83.89E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: unidentified gas infrastructure in West Siberian taiga

sron_20260622_65.98N_74.18E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The DKS-3 (ДКС-3) booster compressor station in Russia's Medvezhye gas field is the most likely source of this 104,000 kg/hr methane plume. The facility sits 6.7 km south of the TROPOMI plume centroid — within the expected 2–10 km offset for this sensor — and lies in the general upwind direction (wind was from the southeast at 3.7 m/s on the detection date). A mapped flare and storage tanks at the DKS-3 coordinates confirm active gas-handling infrastructure, and booster compressor stations are well-documented large methane emitters, particularly during blowdowns or seal failures. The Medvezhye field has a persistent methane record: the detection history shows 12 prior satellite detections within 30 km, including five high-resolution GHGSat observations clustered 24 km SSE and multiple TROPOMI detections at 30,000–155,000 kg/hr across 2023–2025, indicating chronic emissions from the field's ageing infrastructure operated by Gazprom Mining Nadym. Attribution confidence is limited to medium because TROPOMI's 5.5×7 km pixels cannot resolve individual facilities and OpenStreetMap infrastructure mapping is sparse in this remote Siberian field.
sron_20260622_65.98N_74.18E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Medvezhye gas field compressor station venting

sron_20260623_10.21N_71.32W|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Oil and gas infrastructure in Venezuela's Lagunillas field is the likely source of this 66,000 kg/hr methane plume. The TROPOMI detection sits on the eastern shore of Lake Maracaibo within the actively licensed BACHAQUERO TIERRA-LAGUNILLAS TIERRA block operated by PETROZAMORA (PDVSA Group). An OGIM-catalogued gas collection station lies 1.4 km to the north-northwest — downwind under the very light southerly wind (0.1 m/s) — and is the closest identified gas-handling facility, though TROPOMI's 5.5×7 km pixel likely integrates emissions from multiple well pads, flowlines, and platforms across the field. The attribution is reinforced by 30 other satellite detections within 30 km since 2024, including GHGSat and EnMAP observations exceeding 12,000 kg/hr that confirm persistent, high-volume methane releases from this sector of the Maracaibo Basin.

sron_20260623_33.51N_101.97W|SRON_Weekly.paragraph: A TROPOMI-detected methane plume of 16,000 kg/hr was observed on 23 June 2026 near southwest Lubbock, Texas (33.51°N, 101.97°W). With surface wind from the southeast, the source is expected 2–10 km upwind (southeast) of the reported coordinate, yet the southeast sector contains only plugged dry holes, a shut-in well, and farmyards — none capable of producing a plume of this magnitude. Potential methane sources exist elsewhere within the 15 km search radius — including a landfill 14.6 km east-northeast, a decommissioned gas-fired power plant (Brandon Station, closed 2023) 11 km northeast, and several petroleum wells 6–14 km west and northwest — but none align with the reported wind direction. Three prior TROPOMI detections in the Lubbock area (63,000–105,000 kg/hr in 2025–2026) confirm that one or more very large persistent methane sources operate in the region, likely including the Caliche Canyon Landfill 21 km north-northeast (identified as a waste-sector emitter by Carbon Mapper in 2023), but the specific source of this plume could not be determined from the available evidence.
sron_20260623_33.51N_101.97W|SRON_Weekly.source_label: Unattributed large methane plume southwest of Lubbock

sron_20260623_41.22N_68.94E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: A large waste landfill at 41.150°N, 68.932°E — labelled 'Полигон отходов' (Waste landfill) in OpenStreetMap — is the likely source of this TROPOMI methane plume. The landfill centre sits 7.8 km south (upwind) of the reported plume coordinate, within the 2–10 km offset typical for TROPOMI detections, and the southerly wind on 23 June 2026 would carry its emissions directly over the detection point. The area has registered 125 satellite methane detections between 2023 and 2026, with clusters radiating in all directions from the landfill under varying wind conditions and rates ranging from 6,000 to 103,000 kg/hr — a pattern most consistent with a large, persistently emitting waste disposal site rather than intermittent industrial activity.
sron_20260623_41.22N_68.94E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Waste landfill south of Keles border area

sron_20260623_52.10N_74.41E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The Ekibastuz coal basin in northeastern Kazakhstan, specifically the Bogatyr open-pit mine, is the likely source of this plume. The 42,000 kg/hr emission rate is consistent with previously documented satellite measurements of methane from Ekibastuz mines, which have been observed emitting between 27,500 and 54,000 kg/hr — placing them among the world's largest coal mine methane ultra-emitters. Surface wind on the detection date was from the ESE (117°), aligning near-perfectly with the Ekibastuz mines 70–84 km to the ESE of the TROPOMI-detected enhancement. While the source distance exceeds the typical 2–10 km TROPOMI offset, the SRON weekly composite product integrates multiple overpasses, and a plume of this magnitude would remain detectable far downwind; no other industrial sources exist within the typical search radius that could approach this emission rate.
sron_20260623_52.10N_74.41E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Ekibastuz coal basin, likely Bogatyr open-pit mine

sron_20260623_60.45N_120.23E|SRON_Weekly.paragraph: A single TROPOMI detection on 23 June 2026 recorded a methane plume of approximately 18,000 kg/hr at 60.45°N, 120.23°E in the Olyokminsky District of Russia's Sakha Republic. The daily-mean surface wind was from the NNW, placing the likely source 2–10 km upwind in uninhabited taiga within the YAKU 16143 HP hydrocarbon production licence operated by Tuymaada-Neftegaz AO. The same licence hosts the Mukhtinskoye gas condensate field (34.8 billion cubic metres recoverable reserves, discovered in 2023) approximately 92 km to the north-northeast, confirming the area's gas-rich geology. No specific well pad, pipeline, or facility is mapped at the upwind location in OSM or OGIM, and the plume was not detected on any other satellite pass, suggesting a transient event such as well testing, flowback, or an operational upset rather than a persistent source. The ESPO oil pipeline pump station and the town of Olyokminsk lie 10–14 km downwind and are inconsistent with the wind direction.
sron_20260623_60.45N_120.23E|SRON_Weekly.source_label: Gas well or infrastructure in Tuymaada-Neftegaz licence area

sron_20260624_32.62S_151.04E|SRON_Weekly.paragraph: The Mount Thorley Warkworth coal mine in the Hunter Valley, New South Wales, is the likely source of the 18,000 kg/hr methane plume detected by TROPOMI on 24 June 2026. The detection coordinate falls inside the mine's mapped boundary, and the area has a dense record of 199 satellite methane detections — including 23 high-resolution GHGSat and Carbon Mapper observations explicitly tagged as coal-related and located within the mine perimeter. The mine, operated by Coal & Allied (a Yancoal Australia subsidiary), produces approximately 17 million tonnes of coal annually from open-cut operations and reports methane emissions under Australia's National Greenhouse and Energy Reporting scheme. Published research has identified Hunter Valley coal mines, including Mount Thorley Warkworth, as persistent methane superemitters routinely detected by TROPOMI satellite observations.

sron_20260624_37.49N_61.83E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The Mary State Power Station (Mary GRES), a 3,259+ MW gas-fired power complex operated by Turkmenenergo, is the likely source of this 34,000 kg/hr methane plume. The detection at 37.49°N, 61.83°E sits 6.8 km south of the power station's main site, consistent with the NNE wind (31°) that day — TROPOMI plumes typically originate 2–10 km upwind of the reported coordinate. The area has produced at least 40 TROPOMI methane detections since January 2023 with rates ranging from 25,000 to 182,000 kg/hr, most classified by IMEO as oil and gas sector emissions, and the closest historical detection cluster lies just 1.3 km from the power plant's OSM-mapped footprint. Turkmenistan holds the world's fifth-largest natural gas reserves and its gas infrastructure is a known source of persistent large methane leaks.
sron_20260624_37.49N_61.83E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Mary State Power Station gas-fired complex

sron_20260624_42.18N_60.33E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: A gas pipeline in the Gazli-Nukus trunkline system is the likely source of this 75,000 kg/hr methane plume. The TROPOMI detection on 24 June 2026 at 42.18°N, 60.33°E sits downwind (ESE) of WNW winds at 1.3 m/s, pointing to a source in the WNW–NW corridor. Unnamed underground gas pipeline spurs (OSM ways 475637654/475637655) lie 6–8 km upwind — within the expected 2–10 km TROPOMI source offset — and converge near 42.226°N, 60.268°E on a route consistent with a branch from the Gazli-Nukus trunkline. The area has produced at least nine other large TROPOMI methane plumes since 2023 (rates from 17,000 to 150,000 kg/hr), confirming a persistent gas-infrastructure emission hotspot. An unnamed 34-hectare industrial facility at 1.2 km NW (way/1374233161), possibly the gas-fired thermal power plant under construction for the Tebinbulak mining complex, is an alternative candidate but lies closer than the typical TROPOMI source distance.

sron_20260624_43.72N_1.46E|SRON_Weekly_M.note: The landfill at OSM way/1281146726 was mapped in May 2024 from BDOrtho IGN aerial imagery and has no name, operator, or verification as a municipal solid waste (rather than inert) facility. The Terega gas transmission network operates multiple 'Poste Gaz' substations and underground pipelines throughout the area, and a pipeline blowdown or maintenance vent at one of these could also explain a 10 t/hr one-off emission, though wind alignment favours the landfill.
sron_20260624_43.72N_1.46E|SRON_Weekly_M.paragraph: An unnamed landfill mapped in OpenStreetMap approximately 12 km east-southeast of the TROPOMI detection coordinate is the most plausible source, based on wind direction (ESE at 1.8 m/s placing the source nearly perfectly upwind at bearing 106°) and the emission rate of 10,000 kg/hr, which is consistent with a large municipal waste disposal site. However, the landfill is slightly beyond TROPOMI's typical 2–10 km source offset, bears no name or operator in OSM, and was mapped from aerial imagery without site verification — it could be an inert construction-waste facility producing little methane. No repeat detections exist in the 30 km archive, which could indicate either a one-off event or that this is not a persistent methane source. Alternative candidates include Terega gas pipeline substations in the area (the nearest at 1.3 km SSE), though these lie well outside the upwind corridor.
sron_20260624_43.72N_1.46E|SRON_Weekly_M.source_label: Unnamed landfill near Gragnague, east of Toulouse

sron_20260624_54.12N_87.34E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The 43,000 kg/hr methane plume detected by TROPOMI on 24 June 2026 is most consistent with coal mine methane venting from the Yerunakovskaya-8 underground coal mine, operated by Raspadskaya (Evraz). Surface wind was from the east at 0.7 m/s, and the mine's main infrastructure sits 1.0 km east-northeast of the plume coordinate — almost exactly upwind (bearing 77°, only 9° off the wind direction). The mine is a longwall operation with at least nine documented methane source points including ventilation shafts and gas drainage stations, and it has a history of methane safety violations — in February 2023 operations were suspended after methane concentrations exceeded permissible limits fourfold. The Yerunakovo mining area is one of the most persistently observed methane hotspot regions in the satellite record, with 199 detections within 30 km in the archive, including a TROPOMI detection of 42,000 kg/hr just four days earlier (20 June 2026) and Carbon Mapper routinely resolving individual shaft-level plumes of 100–4,500 kg/hr across the mine's 8 km² lease.

sron_20260624_63.96N_122.44E|SRON_Weekly.operator: Yakutsk Fuel and Energy Company OJSC (YATEC)
sron_20260624_63.96N_122.44E|SRON_Weekly.paragraph: A gas production or compression facility within the Srednevilyuyskoye gas-condensate field is the likely source of this 22,000 kg/hr methane plume. The TROPOMI detection coordinate (63.96°N, 122.44°E) lies within the developed area of the field, which is operated by YATEC (Yakutsk Fuel and Energy Company) in the Lena-Vilyuy Basin of Sakha Republic. Satellite imagery confirms significant industrial clearing at and around the detection coordinate, and MapStand data maps 20 production wells within 4–11 km to the south and southeast. The northerly wind on the detection day (from 354° at 3 m/s) is consistent with a source at or just north of the coordinate within the field's northern infrastructure. The very high emission rate suggests a major venting, blowdown, or flaring event rather than a routine well leak, and a prior GHGSat detection in May 2023 (3,256 kg/hr, 11 km ESE) confirms this field has a history of significant methane releases.

sron_20260625_50.21N_18.76E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Methane venting from the Szyb V (Shaft V) ventilation system of the KWK Budryk underground coal mine, operated by JSW SA, is the likely source of this TROPOMI detection. The emission rate of 32,000 kg/hr (±15,000) is consistent with a large underground coal mine ventilation shaft; the TROPOMI pixel (5.5 × 7 km) integrates methane from the mine complex, and the very light NW wind (0.8 m/s) allowed the plume to spread across the area. This shaft is one of the most persistently detected methane sources in the satellite archive, with 36 prior detections since 2022 by GHGSat, Carbon Mapper, EMIT, PRISMA and EnMAP at rates ranging from 310 to 3,940 kg/hr — the most recent being a PRISMA detection of 1,396 kg/hr on 6 May 2026, only seven weeks earlier. An additional three GHGSat detections at the mine's Szyb VI shaft (0.9 km SSE, 380–815 kg/hr) confirm that the broader Budryk mine complex is a major and sustained source of coal mine methane.
sron_20260625_50.21N_18.76E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: KWK Budryk coal mine ventilation shaft V

sron_20260625_67.76N_82.24E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: A large methane plume of 28,000 kg/hr was detected by TROPOMI on 25 June 2026 over the remote Turukhansky District of Krasnoyarsk Krai, Siberia, but the source cannot be confidently identified. Wind was from the east, pointing to a source 2–10 km east of the detection coordinate, yet satellite imagery reveals only pristine tundra with no visible well pads, roads, or pipeline corridors in the search area. The only mapped infrastructure nearby is the North Tukolandsky 1 exploration well 5.2 km to the northwest, but the wind direction makes it an unlikely candidate. The area sits within the hydrocarbon-rich West Siberian Basin near Rosneft's Vankor cluster, so an unmapped gas pipeline, exploration well test, or temporary infrastructure could explain the emission, but no specific source can be attributed with the available evidence.
sron_20260625_67.76N_82.24E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: unknown source in remote West Siberian tundra

sron_20260625_67.87N_81.43E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: A large methane plume (17,000 kg/hr) detected by TROPOMI on 25 June 2026 in the remote Tazovsky Rayon of Arctic Russia is most consistent with oil and gas infrastructure operated by LUKOIL-Western Siberia. The plume location falls within the company's SLKH 13249 NE licence area in the West Siberian petroleum basin. Surface winds were from the east at 2.9 m/s, placing the likely source 2–10 km east of the reported coordinate. The emission rate is characteristic of a gas production or processing facility, but no specific named facility could be identified: the area is extremely remote, with no infrastructure catalogued in OGIM or OpenStreetMap, and high-resolution satellite imagery shows no visible surface installations at the mapped location. No other satellite detections have been recorded within 30 km, suggesting this may be an intermittent operational emission rather than a persistent source.
sron_20260625_67.87N_81.43E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Gas infrastructure in LUKOIL's SLKH 13249 NE licence

sron_20260626_35.48S_59.12W|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: A landfill or municipal waste dump near Carlos Beguerie in rural Buenos Aires province is the most likely source of this plume. The TROPOMI detection on 26 June 2026 measured 123,000 kg/hr — an exceptionally high rate — with a NNE wind placing the source 2–10 km upwind of the reported coordinate (−35.48, −59.12). IMEO classified three earlier TROPOMI detections in the same area (84,000–86,000 kg/hr in May 2024, 55,000 kg/hr in May 2025, and 69,000 kg/hr in September 2025) as 'waste' sector sources, and no oil and gas infrastructure or coal mines exist within the search radius. The specific facility could not be identified: OpenStreetMap mapping in this part of Buenos Aires province is sparse, and web searches did not return a named operator. The repeated detection history and consistent 'waste' classification by IMEO strongly support a landfill origin, though on-the-ground verification is needed to identify the precise site and operator.
sron_20260626_35.48S_59.12W|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Unnamed landfill or waste dump near Carlos Beguerie, Buenos Aires

sron_20260626_38.36N_66.18E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The 12,000 kg/hr TROPOMI detection on 26 June 2026 is most consistent with emissions from gas production infrastructure in the Tandyrcha gas field, part of Lukoil's South-West Gissar project in Uzbekistan's Qashqadaryo Region. The detection sits downwind (east) of a dense cluster of over 30 satellite methane detections spanning 2022–2025 and multiple sensors — including Carbon Mapper, EMIT, EnMAP, PRISMA, and TROPOMI — all classified as oil and gas and centred roughly 19–23 km northwest of this plume coordinate. A westerly wind of 0.9 m/s on the detection day would carry emissions from that production zone toward the observed plume location, and the 12,000 kg/hr rate falls between individual high-resolution sensor readings (400–4,800 kg/hr) and earlier TROPOMI measurements over the same field (48,000–148,000 kg/hr), consistent with an aggregate signal from multiple well pads and gathering infrastructure. No coal mines, landfills, or other industrial sources are present in the upwind search area, and the MapStand database identifies a 30.7 km² Tandyrcha gas accumulation at this location within the Afghan-Tajik Basin.
sron_20260626_38.36N_66.18E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Tandyrcha gas field production infrastructure, South-West Gissar

sron_20260626_41.35N_69.08E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The Chiqindi poligoni municipal landfill complex, 3.7 km WNW of the TROPOMI detection at 41.35°N 69.08°E, is the most likely source of this 26,000 kg/hr methane plume. The landfill sits well within the 5.5×7 km TROPOMI pixel and wind on the detection date was nearly calm (0.1 m/s from the SW), meaning the plume would not have drifted far. A prior SRON TROPOMI detection on 17 March 2023 placed a 29,000 kg/hr plume just 1.1 km from the landfill centre, and the 27-date detection history spanning 2023–2026 shows persistent emissions at a mean rate of ~29,000 kg/hr — consistent with a large municipal solid waste site. Several IMEO detections in the area are also classified as 'waste' sector. Given TROPOMI's coarse resolution the exact emission point within the landfill complex cannot be pinpointed, but no other facility within the search radius matches the scale and persistence of the observed emissions.

sron_20260627_31.12N_49.39E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Oil and gas infrastructure in the Marun field — Iran's second-largest onshore oil field — is the likely source of this 22,000 kg/hr methane plume. The TROPOMI detection sits downwind (ESE) of a persistent emission cluster at approximately 31.13°N, 49.32°E, where Carbon Mapper, EMIT, and multiple TROPOMI sensors have recorded 148 detections over three years at rates reaching 100,000 kg/hr. The WNW wind on the detection date places the source upwind of the plume coordinate, directly over this cluster, which lies roughly 800 metres east of the mapped Marun 3 oil and gas exploitation facility operated by NISOC. The emission rates and persistence are consistent with gas flaring, venting, or processing losses at a major oil production complex.
sron_20260627_31.12N_49.39E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Marun oil field production infrastructure, Marun 3 area

sron_20260627_33.95N_113.32E|SRON_Weekly.paragraph: The Tian'an No.13 underground coal mine is the likely source of this methane plume. The TROPOMI detection sits 9.4 km NNW of the mine — consistent with the southerly wind (175°, 1.7 m/s) that would carry ventilation emissions northward across the Pingdingshan coalfield. The estimated emission rate of 19,000 kg/hr is within the expected range for ventilation air methane from a large gassy underground mine producing 2.1 million tonnes of bituminous coal per year. The area has a dense detection history: 120 satellite observations within 30 km, with the UN IMEO consistently categorising them as coal-related, and high-resolution Tanager and EMIT sensors have pinpointed persistent methane from ventilation shafts elsewhere in the same mining complex.
sron_20260627_33.95N_113.32E|SRON_Weekly.source_label: Tian'an No.13 underground coal mine, Pingdingshan coalfield
