sron_20260627_34.01N_71.56E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: A waste disposal site — most likely a municipal solid waste landfill — in eastern Peshawar is the likely source of this methane plume. The plume was detected by TROPOMI at 34.01°N, 71.56°E on 27 June 2026 with an estimated rate of 11,000 kg/hr. The UN IMEO/MARS system has consistently classified 41 repeat TROPOMI detections in this area since 2023 as 'waste' sector, with the detection cluster centred around 34.00°N, 71.59°E — approximately 4 km east-southeast of the current plume, consistent with the light ENE wind carrying the plume toward the detection coordinate. Emission rates across the time series (11,000–41,000 kg/hr) are consistent with a large landfill serving a city of over two million. The Shahlimar wastewater treatment plant (34.03°N, 71.54°E) is the nearest mapped waste-sector facility but lies NNW of the detection, making it a less likely source for this particular overpass given the wind direction. No landfill is mapped in OpenStreetMap at the detection cluster location, preventing a more precise attribution.
sron_20260627_34.01N_71.56E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: waste disposal site in eastern Peshawar

sron_20260627_50.30N_18.46E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Ventilation shafts of the KWK Knurów-Szczygłowice coal mine are the likely source. The TROPOMI detection sits 17.4 km downwind of the mine's Szczygłowice shaft complex — wind on 27 June 2026 was from the SE at just 0.7 m/s, placing the detection almost perfectly on the plume drift axis (bearing 321° from the source, wind blowing toward 322°). The mine, operated by JSW, is one of Europe's largest methane emitters: Poland reported 7,413 kt of methane from this single mine in 2024 (~846,000 kg/hr on average), making the 24,000 kg/hr plume entirely consistent with its normal ventilation. The attribution is reinforced by 25 high-resolution detections (GHGSat, Carbon Mapper Tanager, EMIT, EnMAP) from eight different sensors at the same Szczygłowice shafts between 2023 and 2026, all classified as coal-mine methane — one of the most persistently observed emission clusters in the European satellite record.
sron_20260627_50.30N_18.46E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: KWK Knurów-Szczygłowice coal mine ventilation shafts

sron_20260628_37.16N_5.89W|SRON_Weekly_M.paragraph: The Montemarta-Cónica landfill in Alcalá de Guadaíra is the likely source of this 10,000 kg/hr methane plume. Fifteen prior satellite detections from Carbon Mapper, IMEO (EMIT, EnMAP, TROPOMI), and SRON between 2023 and 2026 form a tight cluster at the landfill — all tagged as waste-sector emissions, with rates ranging from 759 to 13,000 kg/hr, fully consistent with the current observation. The TROPOMI coordinate lies 7 km south of the landfill; while surface winds were from the south-west, TROPOMI's coarse 5.5×7 km pixels produce coordinate scatter of up to 15 km for this source across prior detections. Ecologistas en Acción has described the landfill's situation as 'gravísima e insostenible' (extremely serious and unsustainable), and the site hosts a biomethane injection plant, confirming significant landfill gas generation. No other methane source — no coal mines, no oil and gas infrastructure — exists within the 15 km search radius.
sron_20260628_37.16N_5.89W|SRON_Weekly_M.source_label: Montemarta-Cónica landfill, Alcalá de Guadaíra, Seville
sron_20260628_37.16N_5.89W|SRON_Weekly_M.source_name: Centro de Tratamiento de Residuos Montemarta - Cónica

sron_20260628_44.37N_26.68E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: No methane-emitting facility could be confidently linked to this 3,000 kg/hr TROPOMI plume detected on 28 June 2026 near Gurbănești, Călărași, Romania. The daily-mean wind was from the south-west, so the source should lie roughly 2–10 km south-west of the reported coordinate (44.37°N, 26.68°E), yet that upwind sector is almost entirely agricultural land with no mapped landfills, wastewater plants, coal mines, or oil and gas infrastructure. An unnamed landfill mapped in OpenStreetMap (way/1430879284) sits 6 km to the north-north-west, but wind from the SW would carry its plume to the north-east — nearly perpendicular to the SSE bearing from the landfill to the detection coordinate — making it an unlikely source. No repeat detections have been recorded at this location. The plume may originate from an unmapped source such as an unregistered waste dump, agricultural biogas, or wetland emissions in the Mostiștea valley.
sron_20260628_44.37N_26.68E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Unidentified — no clear source upwind of detection

sron_20260629_35.39N_51.17E|SRON_Weekly_.operator: Tehran Municipality Organization of Waste Recycling and Composting
sron_20260629_35.39N_51.17E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The Aradkouh Waste Processing and Disposal Complex — Tehran's main landfill, in the Kahrizak district about 16 km northeast of the TROPOMI detection — is the most likely source of this 32,000 kg/hr methane plume. Carbon Mapper (EMIT/ISS) high-resolution observations have pinpointed methane escaping from the Aradkouh landfill on six dates between 2022 and 2025 with rates of 2,800 to 4,500 kg/hr; a 2023 Science Advances paper by Thorpe and colleagues explicitly attributed EMIT methane observations to 'the active face of the Arad Kouh landfill near Tehran.' Over 160 TROPOMI detections clustered in this area over the past three years, some exceeding 100,000 kg/hr, confirm a persistent super-emitting source consistent with one of the largest landfills in the Middle East. The 16 km offset between the landfill and the current weekly-composite TROPOMI coordinate, combined with a daily-mean wind from the northwest that would normally push the plume southeast rather than southwest, introduces some uncertainty — the weekly averaging and TROPOMI's coarse 5.5 by 7 km pixels may explain the mismatch, but an unmapped source closer to the detection cannot be ruled out.
sron_20260629_35.39N_51.17E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Aradkouh landfill complex south of Tehran
sron_20260629_35.39N_51.17E|SRON_Weekly_.source_name: Aradkouh Waste Processing and Disposal Complex (مجتمع پردازش و دفع زباله آرادکوه)

sron_20260629_37.13N_120.70W|SRON_Weekly.paragraph: A specific source could not be identified for this 9,000 kg/hr TROPOMI methane detection. The wind was from the northwest at 2.1 m/s, placing the expected source 2–10 km northwest of the reported coordinate (37.13°N, 120.70°W), in a sparsely developed agricultural corridor of Merced County. The upwind search zone contains only plugged oil and gas wells — most notably the MERCED - 1 dry gas well (plugged, Emerald Trail LLC, 4.8 km NW) — and National Wildlife Refuge maintenance facilities; no active landfills, dairies, or industrial gas infrastructure are mapped there. Three other TROPOMI detections at comparable rates (4,000–18,000 kg/hr) span the broader region, and the UN IMEO classified one as 'waste' sector, suggesting a persistent but unmapped agricultural or waste-related source such as a large dairy complex, composting operation, or managed wetland in the San Luis NWR area. Without higher-resolution imagery or ground surveys, the plume cannot be confidently attributed to any specific facility.
sron_20260629_37.13N_120.70W|SRON_Weekly.source_label: Unidentified source in rural Merced County

sron_20260629_39.40N_53.79E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Oil and gas production infrastructure operated by Türkmennebit in the Barsagelmez/Koturtepe fields of western Turkmenistan is the likely source. Carbon Mapper high-resolution satellite detections from 2026 pinpoint a persistent methane source at 39.382°N, 53.806°E, within the Barsa Gelmes oil and gas accumulation. The enormous emission rate of 251,000 kg/hr detected by TROPOMI on 29 June 2026 — with wind from the northwest — is consistent with the known pattern of massive, chronic methane venting from aging Soviet-era oil and gas infrastructure in this region, where an archive of 199 satellite detections within 30 km confirms persistent large-scale emissions. The Guardian reported in May 2023 that Türkmennebit's western Turkmenistan operations — specifically naming the Goturdepe and Barsa-gelmez fields — were the world's worst for methane emissions, with extinguished flares and leaking pipelines venting directly to the atmosphere.
sron_20260629_39.40N_53.79E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Barsagelmez oil and gas field, western Turkmenistan

sron_20260629_63.74N_67.03E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: A gas transmission pipeline crossover (перемычка) and associated looping pipelines operated by Gazprom Transgaz Yugorsk, approximately 3 km north of the detected plume coordinate, is the likely source. The TROPOMI detection on 29 June 2026 measured 15,000 ± 5,000 kg/hr of methane, and surface winds from the NNW place the source directly over a corridor of high-pressure (74 atm, 1420 mm diameter) underground gas pipelines that run north–south through this remote stretch of the Beloyarsky District. No other industrial facilities, landfills, coal mines, or oil and gas wells are mapped upwind of the plume. Four other TROPOMI detections between 2023 and 2025 at different points along the same pipeline corridor — including 23,000 kg/hr 10 km to the south in August 2025 and 38,000 kg/hr 26 km to the east in July 2025 — indicate recurrent large methane releases from this transmission system, consistent with intermittent venting or maintenance blowdowns.
sron_20260629_63.74N_67.03E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Gazprom gas transmission pipeline venting near Kazym

sron_20260630_30.53N_101.26W|SRON_Weekly.paragraph: The plume is most consistent with methane emissions from the dense Montgomery gas field in Crockett County, Texas. A TROPOMI detection on 30 June 2026 measured approximately 122,000 kg/hr at 30.53°N, 101.26°W, with SSE winds placing the likely source area 2–10 km upwind (SSE) of the reported coordinate. The search area contains exclusively gas wells and underground gathering pipelines — no landfills, coal mines, dairies, or processing plants were identified in OpenStreetMap or the OGIM inventory. Within 3 km of the coordinate, 60 gas wells are operated primarily by Scout Energy Management (27 wells) and Bedrock Production (18 wells), together with gathering systems run by Epic Permian Operating and DCP Operating Company. The emission rate is exceptionally high and likely reflects aggregate emissions from multiple well pads within the large TROPOMI pixel, possibly including abnormal venting or an unlit flare; no single facility can be isolated as the definitive source.
sron_20260630_30.53N_101.26W|SRON_Weekly.source_label: Montgomery gas field well cluster, Crockett County

sron_20260630_34.81S_58.75W|SRON_Weekly_.operator: CEAMSE (Coordinación Ecológica Área Metropolitana Sociedad del Estado)
sron_20260630_34.81S_58.75W|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The CEAMSE González Catán landfill is the likely source of this 111,000 kg/hr methane plume. The TROPOMI detection coordinate sits about 8.5 km southwest of the landfill, and the day's wind was blowing from the northeast — placing the landfill directly upwind, exactly where the source must lie for a TROPOMI detection. The landfill is one of four active waste complexes operated by CEAMSE, the Buenos Aires metropolitan waste authority, receiving some 45,000 tonnes of municipal waste per month from a population of 2.3 million. An archive of 133 satellite detections within 30 km shows a dense, persistent cluster of high-resolution plumes (EMIT, EnMAP, Tanager, ISS) directly over the landfill footprint, many explicitly tagged as 'waste' by the detecting agencies — confirming it as a major, long-standing methane source.
sron_20260630_34.81S_58.75W|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: CEAMSE González Catán landfill, Buenos Aires

sron_20260630_36.42N_112.91E|SRON_Weekly.paragraph: A coal mine ventilation shaft or coal-related industrial facility near Zhangcun hamlet in Xiangyuan County, Shanxi, is the likely source of this methane plume. The TROPOMI detection at 31,000 kg/hr on 30 June 2026 is centred 2.5 km west of a tight cluster of 199 satellite detections recorded by Carbon Mapper, EMIT, PRISMA, and EnMAP between 2023 and 2026 — all tagged as coal-sector emissions — at an unnamed industrial compound (OSM way/1118849714) at 36.415°N, 112.937°E. Emission rates at this cluster range from 800 to 11,000 kg/hr across high-resolution sensors, consistent with persistent ventilation of an underground coal mine. The site sits in the Qinshui Basin, one of China's most methane-intensive coal regions, surrounded by several Lu'an Group mines including Changcun (6.7 km southeast) and Yuwu (7.7 km southwest), though the specific facility is not named in available databases.
sron_20260630_36.42N_112.91E|SRON_Weekly.source_label: Coal mine ventilation shaft near Zhangcun, Qinshui Basin

sron_20260630_37.80N_53.84E|SRON_Weekly_.operator: Türkmennebit / DEA Deutsche Erdoel AG (Harbour Energy PLC)
sron_20260630_37.80N_53.84E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Oil and gas infrastructure near a coastal pier in the Korpeje gas field is the likely source of this plume. The TROPOMI detection at 37.80°N, 53.84°E sits 9.7 km SSE of the pier, aligning closely with the daily mean wind from the NNW — plumes from this coastal terminal area would blow directly toward the detection point. Three earlier TROPOMI detections (37,000–290,000 kg/hr) also trace back to the same pier area under northerly winds. The broader area has 199 satellite methane detections on record, with Carbon Mapper and Tanager pinpointing a gas processing facility with gasometers and storage tanks 7 km to the ESE that emits at lower but persistent rates; the coastal terminal and gas plant together mark this stretch of Turkmenistan's Caspian coast as a major, chronic methane release zone within TM Block 23 and the Korpeje field.
sron_20260630_37.80N_53.84E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Korpeje gas field coastal terminal, western Turkmenistan

sron_20260630_38.47N_54.29E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Gas production infrastructure in the Korpedzhe field is the most likely source of this 44,000 kg/hr methane plume detected by TROPOMI on 30 June 2026. The wind was from the NNW, placing the source 2–10 km upwind of the detection coordinate — directly over the northern part of the Korpedzhe gas and oil field, where earlier TROPOMI overpasses have recorded plumes as large as 142,000 kg/hr and where Carbon Mapper's Tanager instrument has repeatedly pinpointed smaller persistent leaks (165–670 kg/hr) from individual facilities. The field, discovered in 1995, is operated by Turkmenistan's state gas company Türkmengaz and supplies the Korpedzhe–Kurt-Kui pipeline to Iran. While the exact emitting equipment cannot be identified from the 5.5×7 km TROPOMI pixel, the 199 prior satellite detections within 30 km confirm this is one of the most persistently methane-leaking regions on Earth, consistent with poorly controlled venting and fugitive emissions from ageing gas production and gathering infrastructure.
sron_20260630_38.47N_54.29E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Korpedzhe gas field infrastructure, western Turkmenistan

sron_20260630_38.81N_53.97E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Offshore oil and gas production infrastructure in Turkmenistan's Block 21 of the Caspian Sea is the likely source of this 127,000 kg/hr methane plume detected by TROPOMI on 30 June 2026. The plume coordinate (38.81°N, 53.97°E) sits downwind of the Block 21 licence area, with NW winds at 4.9 m/s pointing to a source approximately 5 km upwind around 38.83°N, 53.92°E — an offshore location in the South Caspian Basin where prior TROPOMI detections at 59,000–63,000 kg/hr confirm persistent emissions. The detection archive contains 199 satellite-observed plumes across this area since 2023 with rates consistently in the tens to hundreds of tonnes per hour, and high-resolution Carbon Mapper and Sentinel-2 observations pinpoint oil and gas infrastructure emitting nearby at 38.84°N, 54.21°E. The block was previously operated by ARETI International Group, which confirmed its full withdrawal from Turkmenistan by April 2025; operations have likely reverted to the state concern Türkmennebit. The enormous emission rate is consistent with unlit flaring or direct venting from offshore production platforms.
sron_20260630_38.81N_53.97E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Offshore platforms, Block 21, Turkmenistan Caspian Sea

sron_20260630_39.44N_53.73E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The Goturdepe (Koturtepe) oil and gas field in Balkan Province, Turkmenistan, is the likely source of this methane plume. A TROPOMI detection on 30 June 2026 measured 185,000 kg/hr at 39.44°N, 53.73°E, with NNW winds placing the source upwind — directly over the Goturdepe field. This is corroborated by 199 satellite detections since 2023, including high-resolution observations from Carbon Mapper, EMIT, Sentinel-2, Landsat, and PRISMA that pinpoint persistent emissions from well pads and gathering infrastructure within the field, particularly around 39.454°N, 53.717°E. The field is operated by Türkmennebit (Turkmen Oil), which was identified in a 2023 Guardian investigation and Kayrros analysis as the world's worst methane emitter, with extinguished flares and systematic venting documented at its western Turkmenistan fields.
sron_20260630_39.44N_53.73E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Goturdepe oil and gas field venting, western Turkmenistan

sron_20260630_47.20N_131.91E|SRON_Weekly.paragraph: No specific methane point source could be identified within the 15 km search radius of this 32,000 kg/hr TROPOMI plume detected on 30 June 2026 near Shangjieji, Fujin City, Heilongjiang. The area lies within the Sanjiang Plain, a vast wetland and rice-growing region, and the upwind (NNE) sector contains only wind turbines, power lines, small villages, and farmland — none of the OGIM, GCMT, or OpenStreetMap databases record any oil and gas infrastructure, coal mines, or landfills within range. The nearest mapped industrial sites are agricultural processing facilities 10–14 km to the ENE, outside the upwind direction and inconsistent with an emission of this magnitude. Given the very light wind (0.4 m/s from NNE) and the absence of any mapped point source, this plume may reflect diffuse wetland and rice-paddy emissions during peak growing season, an unmapped facility, or a retrieval artifact at the edge of the sensor's detection capability.
sron_20260630_47.20N_131.91E|SRON_Weekly.source_label: no identifiable point source in search area

sron_20260630_61.09N_46.42E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The KS-14 Privodino gas compressor station on the SRTO–Torzhok trunk pipeline is the likely source of this 112 t/hr methane plume. Five high-resolution detections from Carbon Mapper (Tanager) and GHGSat in 2023 and 2025 fall within 150–500 metres of the compressor buildings, confirming a persistent emission source at this location. The TROPOMI coordinate lies 2.9 km west of the station, well within the sensor's search radius under the day's light northerly wind. The emission rate is consistent with a major operational release — such as a compressor blowdown or emergency vent — at one of the three KS-14 compressor units operated by Gazprom Transgaz Ukhta that sit along this 1420 mm diameter gas pipeline.

sron_20260630_62.95N_52.96E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: A TROPOMI detection of approximately 22,000 kg/hr on 30 June 2026 at 62.95°N, 52.96°E in the Knyazhpogostsky District of Russia's Komi Republic cannot be attributed to any specific source. The detection sits in remote, uninhabited boreal taiga with no mapped oil and gas infrastructure, mines, landfills, or industrial facilities within the 15 km search radius — only the Ropcha River, small lakes, and wetlands appear in OpenStreetMap. Winds were from the NNE, and the upwind search corridor is similarly empty of infrastructure. The area lies within the Timan-Pechora hydrocarbon basin, so unmapped oil or gas equipment cannot be ruled out, but without any ground truth, a confident attribution is not possible. No other satellite detections exist in the 30 km archive for this location, offering no corroboration.
sron_20260630_62.95N_52.96E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: no identifiable source in remote Komi taiga

evidence: https://www.gem.wiki/w/api.php (Lubu Coal Mine / Muchesu — not tracked by Global Coal Mine Tracker)
sron_20260701_18.97S_26.03E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The 12,000 kg/hr methane plume detected by TROPOMI on 1 July 2026 at −18.97°, 26.03° is most consistent with coal mine ventilation emissions from Zimbabwe's Hwange–Lubimbi coal district, though the attribution carries significant uncertainty. The wind was from the NNE (32°) at 2.6 m/s, and the only known large methane sources upwind are the Hwange Colliery and the Muchesu/Lubu coal project (Contango Holdings), both roughly 80 km NNE — far beyond TROPOMI's typical 2–10 km source offset, but the bearing aligns nearly perfectly. The area within 15 km of the detection is extremely remote, with no mapped infrastructure in OpenStreetMap, OGIM, the Global Coal Mine Tracker, or MapStand, and no prior satellite detections. The plume rate is characteristic of underground coal mine ventilation; a closer, unmapped small-scale coal operation in the Gwayi valley cannot be ruled out but cannot be confirmed with available evidence.
sron_20260701_18.97S_26.03E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: coal mine methane, likely from Hwange mining district

sron_20260701_32.90N_7.73W|SRON_Weekly_M.paragraph: The 39,000 kg/hr TROPOMI methane plume detected on 1 July 2026 near Lahouaza in Settat Province, Morocco, most likely originates from an unmapped waste disposal site or landfill, but the specific facility cannot be identified with confidence. Surface winds were from the NNE, placing the probable source 2–10 km upwind in a largely agricultural corridor between Lahouaza and the industrial outskirts of Settat; no landfill, oil and gas infrastructure, or coal mine is mapped in this area in OpenStreetMap, OGIM, or the Global Coal Mine Tracker. The emission rate is consistent with a large landfill, and IMEO's methane alert system has separately attributed a persistent TROPOMI detection cluster 25 km to the ENE (33.01°N, 7.50°W) to the waste sector, suggesting waste-management methane sources exist in the region. Without a named facility at the upwind location, this attribution remains tentative and would benefit from higher-resolution satellite follow-up or ground inspection.
sron_20260701_32.90N_7.73W|SRON_Weekly_M.source_label: Unidentified landfill or waste site, Settat Province

sron_20260702_27.30N_95.32E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The 8,000 kg/hr TROPOMI methane plume detected on 2 July 2026 near Naharkatiya, Assam is most consistent with emissions from the Nahorkatiya oil field operated by Oil India Limited. The detection sits amid 37 mapped Oil India Limited wells within 5 km, and a high-resolution Carbon Mapper (Tanager) detection on 8 April 2025 placed a 519 kg/hr methane source just 360 m from well NAHORKATIYA-296 at the same location, confirming persistent oil-field methane at this spot. The site has registered 199 satellite methane detections across TROPOMI and Tanager sensors since September 2023, with rates ranging from 500 to over 58,000 kg/hr — a pattern characteristic of variable emissions from aging oil-field infrastructure including venting, flaring, and fugitive leaks. The specific facility within the field cannot be resolved at TROPOMI's 5.5×7 km pixel scale, but the concentration of repeat detections centred on the Nahorkatiya well array leaves little doubt that oil and gas operations are the source.
sron_20260702_27.30N_95.32E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Nahorkatiya oil field, Oil India Limited

sron_20260702_31.15N_49.15E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Oil and gas infrastructure in the western sector of Iran's Marun oil field, within the Mansureh licence area, is the likely source of this 20 t/hr methane plume. The wind on 2 July 2026 was from the WNW (281°) at 1.4 m/s, placing the source upwind (west-northwest) of the TROPOMI detection coordinate (31.15°N, 49.15°E). A dense cluster of 20 prior TROPOMI detections at 10–79 t/hr lies 6–12 km to the WNW and NW (roughly 31.19–31.22°N, 49.05–49.09°E), confirming a persistent, large methane source in this part of the field. The Marun accumulation is a major producing oil field operated by the National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC), with extensive well pads, gathering lines, and the MARUN pipeline network crossing the area; however, the specific emitting infrastructure at the upwind location is not mapped in OpenStreetMap or the MapStand well database, so the attribution remains at field level rather than to a named facility.
sron_20260702_31.15N_49.15E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Western Marun oil field, Mansureh licence area
sron_20260702_31.15N_49.15E|SRON_Weekly_.source_name: Marun Oil Field (western sector, Mansureh licence area)

sron_20260702_33.72N_6.88W|SRON_Weekly_M.paragraph: A large methane plume (25,000 kg/hr) detected by TROPOMI on 2 July 2026 near Sidi Yahya Zaer, Morocco, is most consistent with a landfill source located 2–10 km northwest of the reported coordinate, based on the prevailing NW wind. A second TROPOMI detection at a nearby location (6 km ESE) in November 2023 supports a persistent source in this upwind corridor. The only named landfill confirmed in the broader region — the CET Oum Azza site serving Rabat, which has been repeatedly detected by higher-resolution sensors — lies 18 km to the NNE and is inconsistent with the wind direction. No landfill or waste facility is mapped in OpenStreetMap at the most likely source location northwest of Sidi Yahya Zaer; the source remains unidentified.
sron_20260702_33.72N_6.88W|SRON_Weekly_M.source_label: Unmapped landfill northwest of Sidi Yahya Zaer

sron_20260702_36.71N_82.42W|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: An unnamed landfill mapped in OpenStreetMap 9.5 km west-northwest of the TROPOMI detection is the most plausible candidate, though the attribution is undermined by wind direction: the daily mean wind was from the north-northeast, which should place the source upwind (north-northeast) of the detected plume, not west-northwest. No methane-relevant sources were found in the upwind corridor, which extends toward the small town of Nickelsville through rural forest and farmland. The landfill's proximity, source type, and the very light wind speed (1.7 m/s) — which can produce poorly defined plume directions — make it the most likely source among mapped candidates, but confidence is low given the wind misalignment. An unmapped source in the upwind corridor cannot be ruled out.
sron_20260702_36.71N_82.42W|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Unnamed landfill near Scott County Waste Transfer Station

sron_20260702_65.87N_77.87E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The Rospan International gas and condensate treatment unit (UKPGiK) and adjacent gas terminal, located approximately 13 km ENE of the TROPOMI detection in the Urengoyskoye field, is the most likely source of this 75,000 kg/hr methane plume. Surface winds on the detection date were from the ENE at 1.6 m/s, placing the facility directly upwind of the plume coordinate, and no other significant methane-emitting infrastructure exists in the upwind direction within the 15 km search radius. The complex includes a flare, multiple gasometers, overground gas pipelines, and a gas terminal — a configuration consistent with the large emission rate observed. A prior TROPOMI detection of a 48,000 kg/hr plume was recorded approximately 21 km east of this location in August 2023, indicating persistent large methane emissions from the broader Urengoyskoye field infrastructure. The 13 km source–plume offset is slightly beyond TROPOMI's typical 2–10 km range, which tempers confidence; however, the perfect directional alignment with wind, the massive emission magnitude, and the absence of alternative upwind sources make this attribution the strongest available.
sron_20260702_65.87N_77.87E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Rospan International gas and condensate processing complex
sron_20260702_65.87N_77.87E|SRON_Weekly_.source_name: Установка комплексной подготовки газа и конденсата (УКПГиК) АО «Роспан Интернешнл»

sron_20260703_34.52S_58.68W|SRON_Weekly_.operator: CEAMSE (Coordinación Ecológica Área Metropolitana Sociedad del Estado)
sron_20260703_34.52S_58.68W|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The CEAMSE Norte III landfill complex is the most likely source of this 28,000 kg/hr methane plume. The TROPOMI detection lies 4.7 km WNW of the landfill's active methane-emitting cell, within the sensor's 5.5×7 km pixel footprint. Eleven high-resolution Carbon Mapper (Tanager and ISS EMIT) detections between November 2023 and June 2026 — all classified as waste-sector — cluster tightly within the unnamed landfill polygon at OSM way/673017156, confirming the source at metre scale. The broader archive counts 199 TROPOMI detections over 2023–2026 at rates of 25,000–88,000 kg/hr, and every IMEO-classified detection is labelled 'waste', establishing a persistent, massive landfill gas source consistent with one of South America's largest municipal waste disposal sites.

sron_20260703_35.66N_51.16E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The Pars Oil Refinery, a 150,000 barrel-per-day crude oil refinery operated by Pars Oil Company, is the most likely source of this 32,000 kg/hr methane plume detected by TROPOMI on 3 July 2026. The refinery sits 10 km NNW of the reported plume coordinate, consistent with the TROPOMI sensor note that the true source lies 2–10 km upwind; the plume and multiple other TROPOMI detections in the archive form a persistent cluster along a SSE axis from the refinery at distances of 10 to 37 km, matching a NNW-to-SSE drift direction across at least seven separate observation dates. No wind data were available for the detection date to confirm drift direction, and the attribution relies primarily on the spatial geometry of the multi-year detection cluster, which points consistently to the refinery rather than to an unregistered landfill 8.5 km to the west that lacks a corresponding detection pattern.
sron_20260703_35.66N_51.16E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Pars Oil Refinery, Tehran province, Iran

sron_20260703_35.74N_43.88E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The Dawd Gurga Gathering Station, operated by North Oil Company in Iraq's Kirkuk oil field, is the likely source of this 39,000 kg/hr methane plume detected by TROPOMI on 3 July 2026. The facility — a manifold and gathering hub for the Kirkuk production network with LPG storage tanks and multiple flare stacks — lies 5.6 km south of the detection coordinate, within the 2–10 km offset typical of TROPOMI. An earlier TROPOMI detection by IMEO in July 2024 recorded a nearly identical 32,600 kg/hr plume just 2 km east, pointing to a persistent large-scale emission from the same area. No wind data were available for the detection date, and the attribution relies on the facility being the only infrastructure of sufficient scale within the search radius; prevailing summer northwesterly winds in the region would place the source south of the detection, consistent with the Dawd Gurga location.
sron_20260703_35.74N_43.88E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Dawd Gurga oil gathering station, Kirkuk field
sron_20260703_35.74N_43.88E|SRON_Weekly_.source_name: Dawd Gurga Gathering Station (محطة تجميع داود كوركا)

sron_20260703_38.23N_53.89E|SRON_Weekly_.operator: DEA Deutsche Erdoel AG / Harbour Energy
sron_20260703_38.23N_53.89E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The 184,000 kg/hr methane plume detected by TROPOMI on 3 July 2026 is most consistent with fugitive emissions from oil and gas production infrastructure within TM Block 23, an offshore and coastal concession in the South Caspian Basin off Esenguly, Turkmenistan. The detection coordinate falls within this active licence area operated by DEA Deutsche Erdoel AG (now part of Harbour Energy), and the region is documented as one of the world's largest methane hotspots — the South Caspian Basin emits an estimated 441 tonnes of methane per hour. The archive of 199 satellite detections within 30 km, including eight high-resolution Carbon Mapper (Tanager) point-source detections clustered at 38.266°N, 54.025°E within the same licence area, confirms a persistent, massive emission source active across multiple years. No wind data was available to refine the attribution, and no alternative sources such as coal mines or landfills exist in the immediate area.
sron_20260703_38.23N_53.89E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: TM Block 23 offshore oil and gas operations
sron_20260703_38.23N_53.89E|SRON_Weekly_.source_name: TM Block 23 oil and gas concession
