sron_20260703_39.16N_53.68E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: Offshore oil and gas production infrastructure in Block 21 of the Turkmen sector of the Caspian Sea is the likely source of this massive methane plume. The detection at 163,000 kg/hr on 3 July 2026 is consistent with a persistent super-emitter hotspot: 199 satellite detections spanning 2022–2026 have been recorded within 30 km, with TROPOMI-measured rates regularly exceeding 100 tonnes per hour. NNW winds place the source 2–10 km upwind of the reported coordinate, within the offshore Block 21 licence area that MapStand records under ARETI International Group, though ARETI publicly confirmed its withdrawal from Turkmenistan by April 2025. Turkmenistan's Caspian offshore has been identified by the UN Environment Programme and Guardian investigations as the world's largest source of methane super-emitter events, with venting from extinguished flare stacks and pipeline leaks cited as the primary causes.
sron_20260703_39.16N_53.68E|SRON_Weekly_.source_label: Offshore oil and gas platforms, Block 21, Turkmen Caspian

sron_20260703_40.40N_3.61W|SRON_Weekly_M.paragraph: The Parque Tecnológico de Valdemingómez, Madrid's principal waste treatment complex, is the likely source of this 5,000 kg/hr TROPOMI methane plume detected on 3 July 2026. The complex — comprising the Las Dehesas and Las Lomas waste treatment plants, the Valdemingómez landfill, an incinerator, and a biogas upgrading plant — sits approximately 7–9 km south of the detection coordinate, well within TROPOMI's 2–10 km source offset. Seven high-resolution GHGSat detections since 2021 (1,000–4,300 kg/hr) fall directly on individual facilities within the complex, and nearly 200 TROPOMI and IMEO detections over four years form a dense cluster over the site, with IMEO consistently tagging the source as 'waste'. The site is a documented methane super-emitter: the UN Environment Programme's IMEO launched a dedicated investigation in 2025, and coordinated ESA–SRON–GHGSat measurement campaigns confirmed persistent, large fugitive emissions from the landfill and biogas infrastructure, with eight major leaks identified since 2023.
sron_20260703_40.40N_3.61W|SRON_Weekly_M.source_label: Parque Tecnológico de Valdemingómez landfill complex, Madrid

sron_20260703_53.86N_87.21E|SRON_Weekly_.paragraph: The 33,000 kg/hr TROPOMI methane plume detected on 3 July 2026 over Novokuznetsk most likely originates from ventilation shafts of the Yubileynaya underground coal mine and the broader Kuzbass mine complex northeast of the city. The area is one of the world's most persistent methane hotspots, with 161 satellite detections in the archive — almost all labelled coal — including a 98,590 kg/hr TROPOMI plume in July 2024 and numerous Carbon Mapper (Tanager) detections at 600–4,600 kg/hr that GEM researchers have specifically attributed to Yubileynaya. The mine, operated by TopProm, has a history of gas-related incidents, including a 2007 explosion that killed 38 miners and a 2023 evacuation of over 140 workers due to gas pollution. Wind was from the northeast at 1.3 m/s, placing the mine cluster — also including Antonovskaya, Bolshevik, and Polosukhinskaya — directly upwind of the detection.

tan20250102t105724c00s4001-A.paragraph: A municipal solid waste landfill near Zéralda, Algeria, is the most consistent source for this plume. Fourteen satellite detections from Carbon Mapper and UN IMEO/EMIT spanning October 2023 to January 2026 — all classified as 'waste' sector and clustered within roughly 300 metres — reveal a persistent, high-emitting source with rates reaching 30,900 kg/hr. No oil and gas infrastructure or coal mines exist within the search radius, and the emission rates are characteristic of a large landfill rather than a wastewater plant or agricultural source. The facility is not explicitly tagged in OpenStreetMap and its official name could not be confirmed through web research, but the evidence pattern — multi-sensor persistence, waste-sector classification, location in a known Algiers waste-shed, and rate magnitude — points decisively to a major landfill, likely the CET (Centre d'Enfouissement Technique) serving western Algiers.
tan20250102t105724c00s4001-A.source_label: Large landfill near Zéralda, western Algiers

tan20251016t113246c82s4001-A.paragraph: The Fos Tonkin LNG terminal is the likely source of this 988 kg/hr methane plume. The Carbon Mapper Tanager detection on 16 October 2025 is located just 66 metres SSE of the terminal — directly downwind of the facility under NNW winds. French environmental outlet Reporterre specifically identified this same October 2025 Carbon Mapper detection as 'une énorme fuite sur le terminal méthanier de Fos-Tonkin.' The detection coincides with a documented strike at the terminal (17 September to 30 November 2025) during which Elengy publicly declared modified emissions. A second Tanager detection nine days earlier (281 kg/hr on 7 October) suggests a persistent emission source active throughout this period.
tan20251016t113246c82s4001-A.source_name: Fos Tonkin LNG Terminal (Terminal méthanier de Fos Tonkin)

tan20260101t053820c53s4001-B.paragraph: Matuail Landfill is the likely source of this 599 kg/hr methane plume. The detection is just 55 metres from the landfill centroid, well within Carbon Mapper's tens-to-hundreds-of-metres precision, and the plume is classified as waste-sector. Eight high-resolution satellite detections (Tanager, EMIT, EnMAP) from 2023 to 2026 cluster within 350 metres of the landfill, with rates of 539–3,713 kg/hr — a persistent pattern consistent with a large municipal landfill lacking gas capture. Wind on the detection day was from the WNW at 1.4 m/s, and a same-day Tanager detection 330 metres ESE of the landfill confirms the downwind drift. No oil and gas infrastructure or coal mines exist nearby, and the only other mapped features within 2 km are a PVC pipe factory, an industrial area, and a water pumping station — none capable of sustained methane emissions at this scale. Published research has specifically quantified greenhouse gas emissions from Matuail Landfill, confirming it as a major and persistent methane source in Dhaka.
tan20260101t053820c53s4001-B.source_label: Matuail Landfill, Dhaka's main municipal solid waste site

tan20260121t184851c40s4001-B.paragraph: An unmapped well pad or gathering facility on Pioneer Natural Resources' Spraberry Driver Unit lease is the likely source of this 6,585 kg/hr methane plume detected by Carbon Mapper's Tanager satellite on 21 January 2026. Carbon Mapper analysts traced the plume origin to 31.6373°N, 101.7632°W, and analysis of the plume mask confirms the source sits at the northern edge of the methane column, with the plume extending southward consistent with the 5.5 m/s northerly wind at the time of detection. No mapped infrastructure exists at this coordinate in either the OGIM inventory or OpenStreetMap, though the nearest recorded wells — the plugged Spraberry Driver Unit 591 (170 m southwest) and the active injection well 1021D (212 m north) — are both on the same Pioneer-operated lease. The emission rate of roughly 8.3 million cubic feet per day is consistent with a major venting or blowdown event. The location lies just 170 metres southeast of the Targa Midkiff Plant property boundary, a 230 MMCFD gas processing facility whose equipment 1.1 km to the north-northwest has generated over 30 satellite methane detections since 2019, but this specific coordinate has no prior detections in the archive, indicating a distinct, intermittent source on the Pioneer lease.
tan20260121t184851c40s4001-B.source_label: Unmapped well pad on Pioneer Spraberry Driver Unit

tan20260607t050236c96s4001-G.paragraph: The Yinchuan Hedong Domestic Waste Landfill (银川市河东生活垃圾填埋场) is the likely source of this methane plume. Carbon Mapper placed the source origin at coordinates that fall inside the OSM-mapped landfill polygon (way/1242834765) in Zhangzheng, Xingqing District. Two other Tanager detections from the same landfill — 500 kg/hr on the same overpass and 257 kg/hr in November 2025 — confirm a persistent methane source at this location. The landfill, operated by the Yinchuan Municipal Administration Bureau, has been a documented environmental concern: a 2022 Ministry of Ecology and Environment inspection found 3.47 million tonnes of accumulated waste, no leachate collection pond, and 230,000 m³ of standing leachate, conditions consistent with substantial ongoing methane generation.
tan20260607t050236c96s4001-G.source_name: 银川市河东生活垃圾填埋场

tan20260607t050236c96s4001-H.paragraph: The Yinchuan City Landfill is the likely source of this 500 kg/hr methane plume. Carbon Mapper's assessed source origin sits just 59 metres from the centroid of an OSM-mapped landfill polygon (landuse=landfill, way/1242834765), well within the sensor's satellite geolocation uncertainty of a few hundred metres. Three Tanager detections spanning seven months — November 2025 (257 kg/hr), and two on 7 June 2026 (564 kg/hr and 500 kg/hr) — all classified as solid waste, form a compact cluster within ~435 m across the landfill, confirming a persistent methane source. The plume mask shows the source coordinate inside the imaged plume and the drift direction (toward SSE) is broadly consistent with the NNE wind at the time of detection. A named OSM node 540 m WNW labels the facility '银川市垃圾填埋场' (Yinchuan City Garbage Landfill). No oil and gas infrastructure or other plausible sources exist within the search radius.
tan20260607t050236c96s4001-H.source_label: Yinchuan City Landfill, Zhangzheng, Xingqing District
tan20260607t050236c96s4001-H.source_name: Yinchuan City Landfill (银川市垃圾填埋场)

tan20260607t063124c38s4001-B.paragraph: The methane plume is most consistent with emissions from the Kaltansky Coal Mine, a large surface mine complex in Russia's Kuzbass basin operated by Kuzbassrazrezugol. Carbon Mapper places the source origin at 53.4326°N, 87.4143°E — an emission point within the mine's ~60 km² operational footprint about 2 km north of the main pit coordinates, with the plume drifting WSW under a light ENE wind, matching the observed mask geometry. The Global Energy Monitor methane tracker explicitly associates this cluster of detections with Kaltansky, and the location has registered seven Carbon Mapper plumes since March 2025 at rates ranging from ~200 to over 2,500 kg/hr, confirming a persistent, high-rate coal mining methane source. The merged Kaltansky–Osinnikovsky operation produced 5.37 million tonnes of coal in 2022.
tan20260607t063124c38s4001-B.source_label: Kaltansky coal mine surface operations or ventilation

tan20260607t063124c38s4001-C.paragraph: The Mezhdurechenskiy Coal Mine is the likely source of this 1,839 kg/hr methane plume. The Carbon Mapper satellite detection places the emission origin at 53.6611°N, 87.9278°E, which falls within the mine's operational boundary (polygon M1271.B1, ~9 km²) and 520 metres north of the mine's centre marker. Twelve additional Carbon Mapper detections have been recorded at essentially the same location between December 2024 and June 2026, with emission rates ranging from 858 to 7,868 kg/hr — a persistent point source consistent with methane liberated from exposed coal seams at an active surface mine in the gassy Kuznetsk basin. The Global Energy Monitor wiki explicitly lists this mine under 'Coal mines with boundaries and methane sources' and associates multiple of these Carbon Mapper detections with it. The mine, operated by Mezhdurechie JSC (part of Novaya Gornaya Management Company), produced 4.3 million tonnes of bituminous coal in 2024.

tan20260607t080825c49s4001-A.paragraph: A well pad or small gas-handling facility within Turkmenistan's Nayyp gas field is the likely source of this methane plume. Carbon Mapper traced the plume origin to coordinates (40.7934, 61.3132), approximately 500 metres east-northeast of the named Nayyp Gas Processing Plant — a distinct and separate location. Five Carbon Mapper Tanager detections cluster tightly at this spot between March 2025 and June 2026 with emission rates of 366–1,454 kg/hr, confirming a persistent source consistent with ongoing gas production infrastructure rather than a one-off event. The plume drifts west-southwest, consistent with the easterly wind recorded at the time of detection. The Nayyp field lies within the Amu-Darya Basin and forms part of the Bagtyyarlyk production-sharing agreement operated by CNPC with Turkmengaz.
tan20260607t080825c49s4001-A.source_label: Nayyp gas field well pad or gas facility

tan20260607t080825c49s4001-B.paragraph: Gas infrastructure within the Nayyp gas field is the likely source of this 1,022 kg/hr methane plume. The Carbon Mapper source origin sits at the southern edge of the Nayyp Gas Field Headquarters compound (OSM way/247027308) in Turkmenistan's Amu-Darya Basin. A repeat Tanager detection at essentially the same coordinate (22 m away) recorded 1,058 kg/hr in November 2025, and five EMIT detections within 75 m recorded rates from 326 to 1,923 kg/hr between June 2023 and October 2024 — together confirming a persistent point source. The plume drifts westward, consistent with the easterly wind recorded at the time of detection. The specific equipment (likely a well pad or gas-gathering station) is not individually mapped in available inventories, and the operating company could not be confirmed, though the location falls within the state-run NALP gas accumulation in the Amu-Darya Basin.
tan20260607t080825c49s4001-B.source_label: Nayyp gas field infrastructure, Darganata, Turkmenistan

tan20260607t080825c49s4001-C.paragraph: A gas well pad or small gathering facility in Turkmenistan's Nayyp gas field is the likely source of this 1,598 kg/hr methane plume detected by Carbon Mapper's Tanager satellite on 7 June 2026. The source origin was placed at 40.8°N, 61.292°E — a location that has produced seven prior methane detections by EMIT and Carbon Mapper instruments since June 2023, with rates ranging from 128 to 1,627 kg/hr, confirming a persistent multi-year source. The site lies within the NALP gas accumulation of the Amu-Darya Basin, where Türkmengaz operates the Nayyp field; the nearest mapped OSM feature is an unnamed industrial area 580 metres northeast, and the Nayyp Gas Field Headquarters sits 1.6 km to the southeast — consistent with unmapped well-pad infrastructure at the coordinate, typical for Turkmenistan's sparsely documented gas fields. Wind from the east at 1.6 m/s drives the plume westward, matching the geometry of the Carbon Mapper plume mask.
tan20260607t080825c49s4001-C.source_label: Gas well pad in Nayyp field, Lebap, Turkmenistan

tan20260607t080825c49s4001-E.paragraph: An unnamed oil and gas facility in Turkmenistan's Amu-Darya Basin is the likely source of this persistent methane plume. The Carbon Mapper Tanager detection on 7 June 2026 measured 501 kg/hr at a source origin coordinate (40.0493°N, 61.0461°E) that falls inside an OpenStreetMap-mapped industrial oil polygon (way 292481605) in the Darganata District of Lebap Region. The site has been detected 176 times by multiple satellite sensors (Carbon Mapper, Sentinel-2, Landsat, EMIT) since 2022, with rates ranging from approximately 300 to nearly 15,000 kg/hr — making it one of the most persistently observed methane sources in the region. The chronic, high-rate emissions are consistent with gas processing or compression infrastructure, though the specific facility name could not be confirmed from available open-data sources. The operator is most likely Türkmengaz, Turkmenistan's state gas company, which controls the majority of gas infrastructure in this part of the Amu-Darya Basin.
tan20260607t080825c49s4001-E.source_label: Unnamed oil and gas facility, Darganata, Turkmenistan

tan20260607t080955c01s4001-C.paragraph: A methane plume detected by Carbon Mapper's Tanager satellite on 7 June 2026 is most consistent with unmapped oil and gas infrastructure at 36.4016°N, 61.3538°E in Turkmenistan's Dovletabad-Donmez gas field. Carbon Mapper assessed the source origin at this exact coordinate, and the plume extended approximately 1.2 km westward, consistent with the easterly wind (99°) of 1.1 m/s at the time of detection. The same location has been detected emitting methane on five previous occasions since August 2023 by both Carbon Mapper and UN IMEO sensors, with rates ranging from 924 to 2,107 kg/hr, confirming a persistent, chronic source. No infrastructure is mapped at this coordinate in OGIM, OpenStreetMap, or MapStand, but the site lies within the producing Dovletabad-Donmez gas field operated by Turkmengas, Turkmenistan's state gas company, and is most likely a well pad or small gas gathering facility.
tan20260607t080955c01s4001-C.source_label: Unmapped gas infrastructure in Dovletabad-Donmez field

tan20260607t080955c01s4001-D.paragraph: A gas well pad or small gas-gathering facility in Turkmenistan's Dovletabad-Donmez gas field is the likely source. A Carbon Mapper (Tanager) satellite detection on 7 June 2026 placed the source origin at 36.3309°N, 61.2718°E with a measured emission rate of 293 ± 59 kg/hr. Satellite imagery confirms cleared well pads and oil/gas infrastructure at the detection coordinate, situated just east of an industrial land-use polygon mapped in OpenStreetMap. The site lies within the Dovletabad-Donmez gas accumulation (Amu-Darya Basin), one of Turkmenistan's largest gas-producing fields, operated by the state company Turkmengaz; ten other satellite methane detections have been recorded within 10 km since 2023, confirming persistent emissions across the field.
tan20260607t080955c01s4001-D.source_label: gas well pad, Dovletabad-Donmez field, Turkmenistan

tan20260607t094218c14s4001-A.paragraph: The Kayseri municipal solid waste landfill (Kayseri Çöplüğü) is the likely source of this 258 kg/hr methane plume. Carbon Mapper placed the emission origin at 38.7823, 35.3087, and classified it as solid waste — consistent with landfill gas. Four Carbon Mapper detections between November 2025 and June 2026 cluster across a ~1.7 km area spanning from the landfill's biogas power plant (Kayseri Çöplüğü Biyogaz Elektrik Santrali, 5.78 MW, operated by Her Enerji) at the northern end to this hotspot at the southern end, with rates of 137–453 kg/hr typical of landfill emissions. The landfill body itself is not explicitly mapped in OpenStreetMap, but the biogas plant and the clustered repeat detections confirm a large active landfill at this location serving the Kayseri metropolitan area (population ~1.2 million).
tan20260607t094218c14s4001-A.source_label: Kayseri municipal landfill (Kayseri Çöplüğü), southern sector
tan20260607t094218c14s4001-A.source_name: Kayseri Çöplüğü (Kayseri municipal solid waste landfill)

tan20260607t094218c14s4001-B.paragraph: The Kayseri municipal landfill (Kayseri Çöplüğü) is the likely source of this 453 kg/hr methane plume. Carbon Mapper placed the source origin at 38.779°N, 35.3158°E — coordinates that Google Maps labels 'Kayseri Çöplük', directly on the landfill body. Four Carbon Mapper detections cluster within 1.5 km of this site across two dates (November 2025 and June 2026), all classified as solid waste emissions, with rates between 137 and 453 kg/hr — a pattern consistent with persistent fugitive methane from landfill waste mass. The landfill's biogas capture plant (Kayseri Çöplüğü Biyogaz Elektrik Santrali, operated by Her Enerji) sits 1.6 km to the north-northeast, confirming the site's identity; the plume drifted SSE, matching the NNW wind recorded at the time of detection.

tan20260607t111256c68s4001-A.paragraph: The Andrzej IX ventilation shaft of the ZG Brzeszcze underground coal mine is the likely source of this 223 kg/hr methane plume. Carbon Mapper's assessed source origin falls within 40 metres of the mapped shaft complex, and the plume mask extends east-northeast, consistent with the WSW wind at the time of detection. This location has been detected emitting methane at least 23 times since 2022 by Carbon Mapper, GHGSat, and IMEO sensors, with rates ranging from 257 to 1,540 kg/hr — a persistent signature of mine ventilation. The Brzeszcze mine, operated by Tauron Wydobycie, is a bituminous thermal coal mine producing 0.66 Mt/year, and Polish news coverage confirms the site is known for methane handling challenges.
tan20260607t111256c68s4001-A.source_label: Andrzej IX vent shaft, ZG Brzeszcze mine
tan20260607t111256c68s4001-A.source_name: ZG Brzeszcze Coal Mine – Szyb Andrzej IX

tan20260607t160334c74s4001-A.paragraph: GM 42, an active oil well in Venezuela's Boca Cachama licence area, is the likely source of the 2,065 kg/hr methane plume detected by Carbon Mapper's Tanager satellite on 7 June 2026. The Carbon Mapper-assessed source origin lies just 129 metres from the mapped well coordinates — well within the satellite's geolocation uncertainty of a few hundred metres — and the plume drifts westward from that point, matching the ESE wind recorded at the time. Four prior satellite detections at the same location between January 2025 and May 2026, with emission rates of 1,417–3,673 kg/hr, confirm a persistent source consistent with an active oil well. The well sits within PDVSA's Boca Cachama licence in the Maturin Shelf basin of Anzoátegui state, where dozens of similarly named GM- and GS-prefix wells indicate a mature, densely drilled oil field.
tan20260607t160334c74s4001-A.source_label: GM 42 oil well, Boca Cachama field, Venezuela

tan20260607t172758c64s4001-A.paragraph: American Landfill, a Waste Management facility at 7916 Chapel St S.E. in Waynesburg, Ohio, is the likely source of the 1,256 kg/hr methane plume detected by Carbon Mapper on 7 June 2026. The satellite's assessed source origin falls inside the mapped landfill polygon — 174 metres from its edge — and Carbon Mapper's own sector classification assigns this plume to solid waste. Wind from the north at 1.9 m/s pushed the plume southward, consistent with the plume mask geometry; the only nearby oil and gas well is a plugged and abandoned well 30 metres west that cannot plausibly emit at this rate. No other satellite detections exist within 10 km in the four-source archive, suggesting this may be a newly observed persistent emission from landfill gas.

tan20260607t172950c47s4001-A.paragraph: A Waste Management landfill in Richland County, South Carolina, is the likely source of this methane plume. The Carbon Mapper satellite detection places the source origin at 34.1058, -80.771 — a point that falls squarely within an OpenStreetMap-mapped landfill polygon (way/512141410) that sits immediately adjacent to a named 'Waste Management' landfill cell. The detection history is decisive: 13 satellite detections from four instruments (Tanager, ISS, EMIT, TROPOMI) between January 2024 and June 2026 all cluster within 400 metres of this spot, with emission rates ranging from 414 to 3,900 kg/hr — typical for a large municipal solid waste landfill. All detections are classified under the waste sector, and the plume geometry is consistent with the westerly wind recorded at the time of detection.
tan20260607t172950c47s4001-A.source_label: Waste Management landfill, Richland County, South Carolina

tan20260607t190302c48s4001-A.paragraph: Equipment at the Lane Gas Plant, operated by Summit Midstream Partners LP, is the likely source of this methane plume. The Carbon Mapper Tanager detection on 7 June 2026 placed the source origin at 32.5333, -103.828, within the plant's industrial property boundary mapped in OpenStreetMap (way/1180911279). Four prior high-resolution detections — two from the Global Airborne Observatory in October 2019 (849–891 kg/hr), one from GAO in May 2024 (287 kg/hr), and one from Tanager in August 2025 (783 kg/hr) — form a tight cluster within 200 metres of this coordinate, confirming a persistent methane source active since at least 2019. The Lane Gas Plant, an operational gas terminal owned wholly by Summit Midstream Partners, is the nearest named facility at 330 metres northeast; the persistent emission rates of 287–891 kg/hr are consistent with midstream gas processing or tank-battery equipment within the plant footprint.
tan20260607t190302c48s4001-A.source_label: Lane Gas Plant, Summit Midstream Partners

tan20260607t190346c80s4001-A.paragraph: A tank battery and well pad on the Johnson W.D. et al lease in Loving County, Texas, is the likely source of this 1,850 kg/hr methane plume. Carbon Mapper's assessed source origin places the emission at 31.7948, -103.5591, which sits between a cluster of seven storage tanks 35–67 metres to the northwest and the Johnson W.D. -E- 2 well approximately 110 metres to the south — well within the satellite's geolocation error. Fourteen repeat detections from airborne and satellite instruments between 2019 and 2026, at rates ranging from 165 to 1,850 kg/hr, confirm a persistent source at this location. No flare has been detected at the site (the nearest VIIRS Nightfire detection is 330 metres northeast at a different well pad), suggesting the emissions stem from tank venting or an unlit flare rather than combustion.
tan20260607t190346c80s4001-A.source_label: Johnson W.D. lease well pad and tank battery
tan20260607t190346c80s4001-A.source_name: Johnson, W. D. et al -E- lease tank battery

tan20260607t190346c80s4001-B.paragraph: A petroleum well pad just north of State Highway 302 in Loving County is the most likely source of this 1,683 kg/hr methane plume detected by Carbon Mapper's Tanager satellite on 7 June 2026. The assessed source origin sits on the highway, with the closest mapped oil and gas infrastructure an OpenStreetMap petroleum well 130 metres to the northeast — well within the few-hundred-metre geolocation uncertainty of the satellite. Winds from the west-northwest at 3.1 m/s are consistent with the plume mask extending east-southeast away from the well pad. Only two other satellite detections have been recorded at this location (IMEO/EMIT in August 2025 at 1,265 kg/hr and IMEO/PRISMA in November 2024 at 1,336 kg/hr), indicating an intermittent source — likely episodic venting or unlit flaring; no VIIRS or Sentinel-2 flare was observed at this coordinate, consistent with cold venting. The well sits among leases operated predominantly by Circle-S Energy, whose nearby JUDGE 3 lease wells reported flaring roughly 4% of produced gas.
tan20260607t190346c80s4001-B.source_label: Oil well pad north of State Highway 302, Loving County

tan20260607t190346c80s4001-E.paragraph: A 256 kg/hr methane plume detected by Carbon Mapper's Tanager satellite on 7 June 2026 is the likely result of an unlit or poorly combusting flare at an oil and gas tank battery on the LUDEMAN D lease, operated by COG Operating LLC in Loving County, Texas. The Carbon Mapper-analyst-assessed source origin coincides with a mapped flare (OSM node 10054286001, within ~17 m of the detection coordinate) and a cluster of storage tanks at the site, and the peak methane column enhancement (1,541 ppb·m) is centered on this location. The plume extends southeast, consistent with the light northwesterly wind (306°, 1 m/s) recorded at the time of detection. The surrounding area hosts numerous COG Operating LLC wells across the LUDEMAN D, SHOCKWAVE, and ECHO leases, with 126 satellite methane detections recorded within 10 km since 2019, though this specific pad has not been detected in prior overpasses, suggesting an intermittent or recently developed emission source.
tan20260607t190346c80s4001-E.source_label: LUDEMAN D lease tank battery flare, Loving County

tan20260607t190346c80s4001-F.paragraph: Devon Energy's MUSKIE 23 11 FEDERAL COM well pad is the likely source of this 704 kg/hr methane plume. The Carbon Mapper instrument assessed the source origin at 32.031, -103.433, which falls directly on the pad — four horizontal oil wells (MUSKIE #007H, #008H, #016H, #035H) sit 50–70 metres to the west-southwest, well within the satellite's geolocation uncertainty of a few hundred metres. All four wells reported production through April 2026, and a nearby tank battery has satellite-observed flare activity. The pad was not previously detected in the 123-survey detection history of the area, suggesting an intermittent emission event such as venting or an unlit flare at the time of the Tanager overpass on 7 June 2026.
tan20260607t190346c80s4001-F.source_label: Devon Energy Muskie 23 11 Federal COM well pad

tan20260607t190346c80s4001-H.paragraph: The Parker B well pad (Parker B – 3H and Parker A Unit – 2H wells), operated by Permian Resources Operating, LLC, is the likely source of this 725 kg/hr methane plume. Carbon Mapper's own analysis places the source origin at the coordinate (31.3308, −103.6155), and analysis of the georeferenced plume mask confirms the highest methane column enhancements cluster at that point, with the plume dispersing southeast under WNW winds of 4.8 m/s at the time of detection. The Parker B – 3H well sits just 74 metres north-northwest of the assessed origin — well within Tanager's satellite geolocation error of a few hundred metres — and the plume mask registers elevated methane (value 64 of a maximum 70) directly over the well. A Carbon Mapper aircraft overpass in October 2019 detected a 1,067 kg/hr plume only 0.34 km to the west-northwest, demonstrating that this pad has been a persistent methane emitter for at least seven years. The VIIRS Nightfire satellite last detected an active flare at this pad in February 2025, suggesting the current emissions may stem from an unlit flare or direct venting rather than combustion.
tan20260607t190346c80s4001-H.source_label: Parker B oil well pad, Reeves County, Texas

tan20260607t190346c80s4001-K.paragraph: An oil and gas facility at an industrial pad mapped in OpenStreetMap (way/1462466004) is the likely source of this methane plume. Carbon Mapper placed the source origin directly at this coordinate, which sits within a mapped industrial=oil land-use polygon just 40 metres away. Seven Carbon Mapper detections cluster within 20–40 metres of this spot between October 2019 and June 2026, with emission rates ranging from 163 to 2,680 kg/hr — a pattern consistent with a persistent but intermittently operating source such as tank venting, separator emissions, or an unlit flare. The nearest named well is COG Operating LLC's Pistol 25-7 2H approximately 290 metres to the northwest, but no specific operator is registered for the pad at the detection coordinate itself; the facility could be part of the Pistol 25-7 lease or operated by a different entity. No VIIRS or Sentinel-2 flare detections coincide with this location, suggesting venting rather than combustion.
tan20260607t190346c80s4001-K.source_label: Unnamed oil and gas pad in Loving County

tan20260607t190346c80s4001-N.operator: EnLink Midstream (Delaware G&P LLC / Delaware Processing LLC)
tan20260607t190346c80s4001-N.paragraph: The 647 kg/hr methane plume detected by Carbon Mapper's Tanager satellite on 7 June 2026 is most consistent with infrastructure within the Lobo gas processing complex in Loving County, Texas. The Carbon Mapper-analysed source origin (31.755, -103.508) falls inside a large OpenStreetMap industrial polygon (way/686864756) that encompasses the Lobo I and II gas processing plants — operated by EnLink Midstream subsidiaries Delaware G&P LLC and Delaware Processing LLC — as well as the MapStand-registered Lobo Processing Plant terminal. No Texas RRC well is mapped within 500 metres of the origin, and the nearest mapped features are storage tanks approximately 150 metres away, suggesting the source is midstream equipment (compressor, tank battery, or process venting) rather than a wellhead. The area is intensely monitored, with 199 satellite methane detections recorded within a 10 km radius since 2019, though this specific coordinate has not been detected before, pointing to an intermittent or newly active source. Attribution carries medium confidence because the exact piece of equipment at the origin coordinate could not be identified from available data.
tan20260607t190346c80s4001-N.source_label: Lobo gas processing complex, Loving County, Texas

tan20260607t190559c69s4001-A.paragraph: The Mazatlán municipal landfill is the likely source of this persistent methane plume. Carbon Mapper classified the emission as solid waste (IPCC 6A), and the site has been detected 11 times between April 2025 and June 2026 at rates of 186–810 kg/hr — a persistent pattern characteristic of a municipal landfill. The Carbon Mapper-assessed source origin sits at the urban fringe of northern Mazatlán where satellite imagery shows extensive disturbed ground consistent with landfill operations, accessed by unpaved roads. The landfill is not mapped in OpenStreetMap (common for Mexican municipal waste sites), and web searches could not confirm the official facility name, but the multi-detection record, waste-sector classification, consistent emission rates, and landscape all point to the city's solid waste disposal site.

tan20260607t190559c69s4001-B.paragraph: The Mazatlán municipal landfill is the likely source of this methane plume. Carbon Mapper's hyperspectral sensor traced the plume back to an origin at 23.2222, -106.3567 on the southern outskirts of Mazatlán, Sinaloa, and classified the emission under IPCC sector 6A (solid waste). Eleven repeat detections by Carbon Mapper's Tanager satellite between April 2025 and June 2026 — all within 0.67 km of the same spot with rates ranging from 186 to 810 kg/hr — confirm a persistent waste-sector methane source consistent with a medium-sized municipal landfill serving a city of approximately 440,000 residents. The observed plume drifted east-northeast, matching the WSW wind of 4.3 m/s recorded at the time of detection. No oil and gas infrastructure, coal mines, or other industrial sources were found in the vicinity, reinforcing the waste-sector attribution.

tan20260607t203336c86s4001-A.paragraph: Coffin Butte Landfill, operated by Republic Services near Corvallis, Oregon, is the likely source of this 697 kg/hr methane plume detected by Carbon Mapper's Tanager satellite on 7 June 2026. The reported source origin sits within the landfill boundary — just 50 metres from the mapped landfill polygon — and the plume mask extends south-southwest, consistent with the NNE wind recorded at the time of detection. This site has been detected emitting methane on 25 separate occasions since July 2023 by multiple satellite and airborne instruments (Tanager, Global Airborne Observatory, EMIT, and TROPOMI), with rates ranging from 405 to over 5,300 kg/hr, establishing a persistent, high-emitting source. The landfill's chronic methane problem is well documented: a 2022 EPA inspection found 61 methane exceedances — 21 of them more than 20 times the regulatory limit — and in November 2025 the Oregon DEQ issued a pre-enforcement notice citing seven Class I violations including an undersized gas collection system and failure to monitor or repair leaks.
tan20260607t203336c86s4001-A.source_label: Coffin Butte Landfill, Benton County, Oregon

tan20260608t043254c92s4001-C.paragraph: TPA Jatiwaringin, a municipal solid waste landfill in Mauk District, Tangerang Regency, Banten, is the likely source of this 543 kg/hr methane plume. The Carbon Mapper assessed source origin falls inside the landfill's mapped footprint (OSM way/513328593), and a second Tanager detection at the same site two months earlier (April 2026) measured a near-identical 547 kg/hr — consistent with persistent landfill methane venting. Both detections are classified under the waste sector. Plume morphology is consistent with the light NE wind at the time of detection, with the plume extending southwest from the origin. The landfill made national headlines in July 2026 when a catastrophic fire — described as an ecological disaster — burned for over nine days, with methane gas explicitly cited by responders as an ongoing hazard, underscoring the site's chronic methane management challenges.
tan20260608t043254c92s4001-C.source_label: TPA Jatiwaringin municipal landfill, Mauk, Tangerang

tan20260608t072546c52s4001-A.paragraph: A ventilation shaft of the Kazakhstanskaya underground coal mine is the likely source of this 1,406 kg/hr methane plume detected by Carbon Mapper's Tanager satellite on 8 June 2026. The source origin coordinate (49.7703°N, 72.5692°E) coincides within ~50 metres with a documented coal mine methane ventilation vent (GEM identifier M1439.P3) catalogued by the Global Energy Monitor, described as a ventilation shaft possibly shared with the adjacent Tentekskaya mine. This location has been detected emitting methane at least seven times since 2023 by Carbon Mapper and EMIT sensors, with rates ranging from 650 to 1,700 kg/hr — a persistent signature consistent with active underground mine ventilation. The shaft sits approximately 2.3 km north of the Kazakhstanskaya mine's main coordinates in the Karaganda coal basin and is operated by Qarmet.

tan20260608t072546c52s4001-C.paragraph: A ventilation shaft at the Tentekskaya underground coal mine (Qarmet JSC, formerly ArcelorMittal Temirtau) is the likely source of this 659 kg/hr methane plume. The Carbon Mapper Tanager detection places the source origin at 49.7967°N, 72.5880°E, where the plume raster shows maximum methane concentration — consistent with a point source at that coordinate in the Karaganda coal basin. The mine's main winding shaft is mapped 0.74 km southeast, but the detection coordinate coincides with an area where a new 830-metre-deep ventilation shaft has been under construction since 2017, approaching the D-6 coal seam; shaft sinking through gassy coal measures liberates substantial methane. Persistent satellite detections at this exact location — at least 10 repeat observations from Carbon Mapper, EMIT, PRISMA, and EnMAP between 2023 and 2026 with rates of 223–1,624 kg/hr, all classified as coal-sector — confirm an ongoing emission source consistent with mine ventilation.

tan20260608t072546c52s4001-D.paragraph: A ventilation shaft of the Tentekskaya Coal Mine is the likely source of this 1,117 kg/hr methane plume. Carbon Mapper's analysts placed the source origin at (49.803°N, 72.5774°E), with the plume mask maximum concentration just one pixel away — the source is at that coordinate. This location lies within the working area of the Tentekskaya underground coal mine (operated by Qarmet JSC, formerly ArcelorMittal Temirtau), and satellite detections have been recorded here on at least four occasions between May 2025 and June 2026 at rates of 558–2,563 kg/hr, consistent with mine ventilation. The Global Energy Monitor independently associates multiple Carbon Mapper plumes in this area with Tentekskaya's ventilation system.

tan20260608t085920c17s4001-A.paragraph: The methane plume detected by Carbon Mapper's Tanager satellite on 8 June 2026 is most consistent with fugitive emissions from the oil storage tank farm at the Balyqshy terminal in the Kalamkas oil field, Kazakhstan. Carbon Mapper's assessed source origin (45.3553°N, 51.8938°E) falls within a dense cluster of over thirty oil storage tanks mapped in OpenStreetMap, with the nearest tank just 31 metres away; the Balyqshy Storage Terminal (MapStand) sits 110 metres east. The plume extends southeast from the source, consistent with the WNW wind (299° at 5.9 m/s) recorded at the time of detection. Four repeat Carbon Mapper detections at this location since March 2025, with emission rates ranging from 400 to 1,760 kg/hr, confirm a persistent methane source at these tanks, which are operated by JSC Mangistaumunaigas, a subsidiary of China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC).
tan20260608t085920c17s4001-A.source_label: Oil storage tanks at Balyqshy terminal, Kalamkas field

tan20260608t085920c17s4001-B.paragraph: A well pad or small oil & gas facility in the Kalamkas oil field is the likely source. Carbon Mapper's Tanager satellite placed the source origin at 45.3795°N, 51.803°E — directly within the Kalamkas licence area (blocks XXX-11-E,F and XXXI-12-D) operated by JSC Mangistaumunaigas, a CNPC subsidiary — on 8 June 2026, with a methane emission rate of 1,398 kg/hr. The plume drifts ESE, consistent with the WNW wind at the time, and the source coordinate sits at a high-concentration pixel within the plume raster. A second Carbon Mapper detection 470 m due east at the same latitude (1,187 kg/hr, March 2025) points to a pair of well pads or facilities aligned along an east–west corridor, a pattern typical of oil-field development. No specific mapped infrastructure exists at the exact coordinate in OpenStreetMap or OGIM, but the nearest mapped feature — a fenced industrial compound 150 m northwest — and the MapStand licence and accumulation records confirm active oil production across this area.
tan20260608t085920c17s4001-B.source_label: Kalamkas oil field well pad, Kazakhstan

tan20260608t090144c24s4001-A.paragraph: The Nazlou landfill, Urmia's municipal solid waste disposal site located roughly 17 km northwest of the city in Nazluchay Rural District, is the likely source of this methane plume. Carbon Mapper's own sector classification assigns the detection to Solid Waste (6A), and the plume origin coordinate (37.7129°N, 44.9716°E) falls within the Nazloochaei/Nazluchay area identified in multiple academic studies as the location of Urmia's municipal landfill. A second Tanager detection 460 metres away on 31 March 2026, also classified as waste at 321 kg/hr, confirms a persistent methane source at this site. The observed emission rates of 300–600 kg/hr are consistent with a medium-sized municipal landfill with inadequate gas capture.
tan20260608t090144c24s4001-A.source_label: Nazlou municipal solid waste landfill near Urmia

tan20260608t120714c63s4001-A.paragraph: The Tivissa municipal solid waste landfill is the likely source of this methane plume. Carbon Mapper assessed the source origin at coordinates just 130 metres from the landfill polygon mapped in OpenStreetMap (way/978048722). Four Tanager satellite detections between May 2025 and June 2026 — all classified as waste-sector and all falling within 50–315 metres of the landfill — form a tight cluster consistent with a persistent point source. Emission rates of 340–890 kg/hr are typical for an active landfill. The plume drift direction (toward NNW) is consistent with the SSE wind recorded at the time of detection. Local news reports confirm the landfill is active and seeking authorisation to expand its capacity.

tan20260608t120845c03s4001-A.paragraph: An unmapped municipal solid waste disposal site serving Mellakou (Tiaret, Algeria) is the most likely source. Three Carbon Mapper Tanager detections clustered within 120 metres of each other over six months (December 2025 to June 2026) confirm a persistent point source emitting 300–470 kg/hr, consistently classified by the sensor's algorithm as IPCC sector 6A (solid waste). No oil and gas infrastructure, coal mines, or mapped industrial features exist within several kilometres; the nearest OSM-mapped features are power transmission towers roughly 1 km away and the village of Biban Mesbah at 2.5 km. The persistent, waste-classified nature of the emissions at this rural location is most consistent with an unregistered communal dump of the type widely used by small Algerian communes, though no formal facility name or operator could be identified from available databases.
tan20260608t120845c03s4001-A.source_label: Unmapped municipal waste disposal site near Mellakou

tan20260608t195144c78s4001-C.paragraph: Coal mine methane infrastructure at the Fording River Operations complex is the likely source of this plume. Carbon Mapper's Tanager hyperspectral instrument placed the source origin at 50.1768, −114.8986 — within a petroleum and natural gas licence (PNG 63361) held by Elk Valley Resources, the same operator that runs the Fording River coal mine 3 km to the northeast. The 3,921 kg/hr plume drifted eastward, consistent with the westerly wind recorded at detection. This location has been detected 52 times by four satellite sensors since 2022, with rates from 34 to over 3,600 kg/hr — the persistence and magnitude are characteristic of coal mine methane drainage or ventilation rather than an intermittent event. The specific infrastructure at the coordinate is not mapped in public databases, but the site sits within the Fording River Operations mining complex in British Columbia's Elk Valley, where Glencore-owned Elk Valley Resources operates several of Canada's largest metallurgical coal mines. The PNG licence covering the coordinate suggests coalbed methane degasification wells may be the source, a practice used to drain methane from coal seams ahead of mining.
tan20260608t195144c78s4001-C.source_label: Fording River Operations coal mine methane drainage
tan20260608t195144c78s4001-C.source_name: Fording River Operations (coal mine methane infrastructure)

tan20260608t195144c78s4001-D.paragraph: A methane plume detected by Carbon Mapper's Tanager satellite on 8 June 2026 at 50.1511°N, 114.9068°W in the Elk Valley, British Columbia, is most consistent with a coal mining emission source. The plume, estimated at 2,637 kg/hr, was traced by Carbon Mapper analysts to this exact coordinate, which lies within the Elk Valley metallurgical coal mining complex. Wind at the time of detection (from the west at 3.7 m/s) is consistent with the plume's eastward drift observed in the raster mask. The detection history records 52 coal-sector plumes within 10 km across multiple nearby clusters, confirming persistent methane emissions across this mining region. MapStand licence data shows the area falls within PNG tenures held by Elk Valley Corporation, the legal entity for what was historically Teck Coal's Elk Valley operations and is now controlled by Glencore. No specific facility is mapped at the coordinate in OpenStreetMap or the OGIM inventory, preventing attribution to a named infrastructure element.
tan20260608t195144c78s4001-D.source_label: Elk Valley coal mining methane source

tan20260608t195144c78s4001-E.paragraph: A coal mine methane source within the Greenhills Operations mining area is the likely source of this 966 kg/hr plume. Carbon Mapper's Tanager satellite placed the source origin at 50.1187, -114.8802, which falls within the Greenhills Operations permit polygon mapped in OpenStreetMap (way/762333037). This exact location has been detected four previous times by Carbon Mapper's AVIRIS-NG aircraft in September 2022, with emission rates ranging from 150 to 491 kg/hr, and the Global Energy Monitor's coal mine tracker explicitly associates those 2022 plume coordinates with the Greenhills Coal Mine. The persistent multi-year detection pattern is consistent with ongoing coal mine methane venting — likely from an exposed coal seam or waste rock dump — at an operating surface mine that reported 588,636 tonnes of methane emissions in 2024.
tan20260608t195144c78s4001-E.source_label: Greenhills coal mine methane vent, Elk Valley

tan20260608t195456c28s4001-B.detection_history_note: Repeat Tanager detection at 0.07 km (413 kg/hr, 2024-09-30); multiple AVIRIS-NG detections at 0.13–0.28 km (158–800 kg/hr, 2016); separate persistent NW cluster at 0.46 km from Bellaire active wells.
tan20260608t195456c28s4001-B.paragraph: A leaking plugged oil well on the historic Kramer lease in the Kern Front Oil Field is the likely source of the 533 kg/hr methane plume detected by Carbon Mapper's Tanager satellite on 8 June 2026. The satellite placed the source origin at 35.4544, -119.0506 — at the northwest tip of a plume that drifts southeast, consistent with the northwesterly wind at the time — a location that sits between the plugged Kramer-4 (70 m southeast) and Kramer-1 (110 m northeast) wells, both former Shell Western E&P operations. A previous Tanager detection at essentially the same location in September 2024 recorded 413 kg/hr, and airborne AVIRIS-NG also detected emissions from this cluster in 2016, confirming a persistent source. The rate is consistent with methane leakage from an improperly sealed or deteriorating plugged and abandoned well, a known problem in California's ageing oil fields.
tan20260608t195456c28s4001-B.source_label: Plugged Kramer well, Kern Front Oil Field

tan20260611t113621c80s4001-A.paragraph: A gas pipeline or associated gas infrastructure within the Polo Petrolchimico di Porto Marghera is the likely source of an 11,426 kg/hr methane plume detected by Carbon Mapper (Tanager satellite) on 11 June 2026. The plume originates at 45.4326°N, 12.2532°E — a point surrounded by overhead gas pipelines (OSM ways 1027457114, 1418752186, 1416110247/48, 1418752175), storage tank farms, and industrial buildings within Venice's historic petrochemical zone. The plume extends 3.7 km to the west-southwest, consistent with the ENE wind (76° at 5 m/s) recorded at the time of detection. A disused 160 MW gas-fired generator sits 91 m west of the source coordinate, and the active 976 MW Enel 'Andrea Palladio' power plant lies 430 m west, indicating dense gas supply infrastructure in the immediate area. The emission, classified by Carbon Mapper as Oil & Gas (IPCC 1B2), is consistent with a major pipeline vent, blowdown, or leak; the absence of prior detections at this location suggests an intermittent operational event rather than a persistent source.
tan20260611t113621c80s4001-A.source_label: Gas pipeline infrastructure at Porto Marghera petrochemical complex

tan20260623t124240c80s4001-A.operator: National Gas Transmission PLC (formerly National Grid Gas PLC)
tan20260623t124240c80s4001-A.paragraph: The Bathgate Compressor Station (mapped as Avonbridge compressor station in OpenStreetMap) is the likely source of this 11,189 kg/hr methane emission detected by Carbon Mapper's Tanager satellite on 23 June 2026. The detection's assessed source origin falls inside the compressor station's industrial boundary polygon, approximately 85 metres from mapped industrial buildings within the complex. The plume extends east-northeast, consistent with the WSW wind (251°) recorded at 4.1 m/s at the time of detection. The emission rate — over 11 tonnes per hour — is characteristic of a major compressor station operational event such as a blowdown or emergency vent, and no other industrial methane sources exist within the search radius.
